utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start, the Chamber is aware that the Prosecution very much wanted to use its time as effectively as possible, and therefore to start in time. It was due to the Martic delay that we have a late start, and I have to even ask you for a couple of minutes more and then, Mr. Harmon, all the time today is yours. I need that time to deliver a decision on the Defence motion for exclusion of appendices A to D of the final brief. On the 25th of August, 2006, the Defence filed a motion seeking exclusion of appendices A to D of the Prosecution's final trial brief on the basis that they contain factual argument and, as such, do not comply with paragraph (C)6 of the Practice Direction of the length of briefs and motions of 16 September 2005. The Defence argues that the appendices are argumentative because they contain summaries of the evidence given in the course of the trial and are referenced only to the evidence which supports the Prosecution's case. Such evidence, according to the Defence, does not purport to be objective and for that reason alone cannot be said to be "non-argumentative," as required by the Practice Direction. The Defence also argues that the Prosecution's claim that the appendices contain "references" is correct only insofar as that term applies to the footnotes, but not to the substance of the text itself. The Defence therefore asks that the Prosecution not be allowed to rely on the appendices; that it be prevented from making any reference to them during the closing arguments; that the appendices be removed from the record; and that the Trial Chamber give an assurance that no use whatsoever is made or will be made of the appendices by the Chamber. On 28 August 2006, the Prosecution filed a response opposing the motion. The Prosecution argues that appendices A to D fall within the wide discretion afforded to the parties by the Practice Direction, as they contain references to relevant transcript pages and exhibits accompanied by "brief non-argumentative contextual information." The Prosecution also claims that there is no requirement in the Practice Direction that a party present material which is relevant to the other side's case. The Prosecution concludes that the fact that an appendix may support the case of the submitting party does not transform that appendix into argumentative material within the meaning of the Practice Direction. The Chamber observes that paragraph (C)6 of the Practice Direction allows for the use of appendices to present "references, source materials, items from the record, exhibits, and other relevant non-argumentative material." Accordingly, it allows the parties considerable discretion as to what to include in the appendices for their final briefs. This discretion is not unfettered, however, and two criteria must be met: First, the material presented in appendices must be relevant; second, it must not contain factual or legal arguments. The use of appendices in final briefs is essentially an exercise in utility. It is meant to enable the parties to assist the Chamber as much as possible in determining a case, while giving them some relief from the word limit. The Chamber's approach to the issue must, therefore, be pragmatic. A final brief is expected to present one side of the case only. Therefore, it would be illogical to insist that the presenting party is only allowed to file an appendix to that final brief if it lists the other party's evidence as well. The fact that the Prosecution may have used its appendices to list evidence that gives support to its case alone does not make them argumentative and is, therefore, not in breach of paragraph (C)6 of the Practice Direction. In addition, in cases such as this one where the Chamber is faced with schedules of alleged crimes, any attempt to associate the scheduled allegations to the evidence received will necessarily involve some interpretation. The Practice Direction should be understood as necessitating that this interpretation be kept to a minimum and that the references to source material are as objective as possible. The unavoidable presence of a degree of interpretation is certainly less problematic in a case such as the present case where the very accused is alleged to be far removed hierarchically from the perpetrators of the crimes on the ground. The Defence does seem to accept that appendices may be used for the purpose of footnoting scheduled allegations to the material in evidence. One could, of course, conceive of appendices consisting only of page references to the original documentation. However, such a document would defeat the ultimate purpose behind the use of the appendices. Accordingly, good reasons should exist for the Chamber to accept the impracticality of such an appendix. The Chamber notes that it's not the first time that a Prosecution final brief is presented with appendices consisting of summaries of evidence. For example, in Prosecutor versus Brdjanin, the Prosecution attached a 70-page annex to its final brief, containing a chronology of events. This chronology included descriptions of alleged crimes, as well as the supporting Prosecution evidence and exhibits. A similar and even longer appendix was submitted in Prosecutor versus Kvocka and others and was accepted by the Trial Chamber. The Chamber has reviewed limited portions of the Prosecution's appendices in order to assess the extent to which, if any, the text contained therein does more than reflect objectively the content of the underlying source material. The Chamber found the text in the appendices to be reflective, as much as that is reasonably possible, of the referenced passages of the source material. Furthermore, the Chamber notes that without the text such as this, which essentially provides a link between the references and the schedules, the appendices would produce only confusion, leaving in doubt the content of the references themselves. Accordingly, the Defence's motion is denied. To the extent that the text included in the appendices A to D contains elements of interpretation of the evidence, the interpretative aspect will be ignored by the Chamber which will, as always, make its own assessment of the evidence cited in the footnotes. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Mr. Harmon, the remainder of the day is for the final argument by the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel. We have come to the conclusion of a very, very long trial, and before Prosecution begins its final submissions, I'd like to publicly acknowledge people who played an important role in the course of this trial. I'd like to start first of all with my colleagues, the lawyers who participated with me, both lawyers from the work in the court-room before Your Honours and who worked behind the scenes in preparing evidence and legal filings in this case. Of course, we couldn't do it without the support of the trial support personnel who assisted us greatly in terms of copying, photocopying exhibits, who in the court-room managed the exhibits, who presented them. The legal assistants who translated -- I should say the language assistants who translated volumes of documents for us. Investigators and analysts. All of them I would like to publicly acknowledge a great debt of gratitude for their efforts. I'd also like to thank Mr. Stewart, Mr. Josse, and members of his team, both past and present, for their courtesy and their professionalism toward the Prosecution which ensured that this trial would move in an orderly fashion. I must say that a great debt of gratitude is due to the people in the language booths, because without them we couldn't proceed, and of course, we lawyers make their lives miserable. We speak too fast, occasionally we go beyond the time we're permitted. The interpreters have to interpret in very, very difficult circumstances. They have interpret victims of crimes whose stories are truly unbearable, and they do the job magnificently. As I stand in this court-room, and I have for many years, this is quite a modern court-room, full of computers and wires and the like, and the technical booth also needs to be acknowledged because they have assisted both parties in the court throughout these proceedings. And for those of us particularly who are technologically challenged, it's been a pleasure working with them and we're indebted. Of course, the members of the registry and the court reporters who have managed efficiently the exhibits we have presented, both sides, the legal filings, production of the transcripts, we're grateful for them -- to them as well. Of course we had numerous witnesses. I think we had 124 viva voce witnesses. A great number of those witnesses, Your Honours, have been assisted by the Victims and Witnesses Unit. They always do their job professionally. We're grateful to them for doing their job in such a competent and professional manner because it gives the witnesses comfort, it gives the witnesses a certain equilibrium before they come into this court-room. That's very important. Of course we thank security as well for their professionalism throughout these proceedings. And finally, I would like to thank Your Honours for the courteous manner in which Your Honours have conducted these proceedings. So thank you. And now we will -- I will describe how we intend to proceed with the arguments. The submissions this afternoon will be made by myself, Mr. Tieger, and Mr. Gaynor. We're going to divide these submissions. There will be occasions when we have to go into private session in order to refer to the testimonies of persons who were protected. Without further ado, Your Honour, I'm going to yield the floor to my colleague Mr. Tieger. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel. Your Honours, in the face of the increasing likelihood that the international community would recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as independent, the Bosnian Serb leadership embarked on a plan to ethnically divide Bosnia by force and create a homogenous Serbian state. In the ethnically intermingled leopard skin that was Bosnia, the objective of a pure Serbian state would have been impossible to achieve without the forcible elimination of non-Serbs even if the territorial aims of the Bosnian Serb leadership had been modest. Their aims, however, were otherwise. The Bosnian Serb leadership sought great portions of Bosnia, including areas where Muslims and Croats were the majority. By the end of 1992, most of those people were gone, cleansed from their homes by Bosnian Serb forces. This case, Your Honours, has been about one of the principal persons responsible for this. Over the course of the case, we have seen and heard witnesses and documents that revealed his position at the apex of the Bosnian Serb political structures and forces through which the objective to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims and Croats was eliminated [sic]. We'd like to begin by having Mr. Harmon and I address certain factual issues in the case that appear to be in dispute. And I'd like to begin with the issues surrounding the objective of the joint criminal enterprise or the common plan. Now, as I just mentioned, the Bosnian Serb leadership opposed an independent Bosnia and sought a separate Serb state on large portions of Bosnia, from which hundreds of thousands of Muslims and Croats, viewed as historical enemies who threatened Serbs, were to be forcibly removed. The leadership assembled the organs and forces necessary to achieve that end, including Crisis Staffs, parallel governmental authorities, and armed forces, and with the recognition of Bosnia at hand, began the forcible ethnic separation of Bosnia and the creation of ethnically pure areas. The Defence asserts that Muslims and Croats were responsible for increasing tensions and were the ones who threatened force to achieve their goals and that Bosnian Serb actions were merely reactive and defensive. They assert that Mr. Krajisnik and other Serb leaders desired peace, that the Bosnian Serb leadership intended only to "retain" territory and did not contemplate involuntary movement of Muslims and Croats. They assert that population movements that occurred thereafter were an inevitable by-product of the war, and that forced movements were not the result of efforts by the Bosnian Serb leadership or done with the knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik. Your Honours, there is of course no dispute that the Muslims and Croats sought the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that Bosnian Serbs opposed it. To contend, however, that Muslims intended to achieve this by a military campaign and that Serb arming and other steps in preparation were a defensive reaction to that intended force is to turn the world on its head. The threat posed by the Muslims and Croats was the political victory of independence. The Defence argument represents the same attempt to blur the lines between political action and physical violence reflected in comments by the Bosnian Serb leadership. See, for example, references by Dr. Karadzic to "constitutional" violence, or his observation that "Violence against the Serb people is called democracy." That's at the 4th Session. The reality was, as Goran Zekic said to the Assembly at the 8th Session on February 25th, 1992, when he was comparing the situation at that time to World War II and the Serb refusal to be -- before World War II to be subjected to subjugation, "Now no one is threatening us with weapons but we have already agreed to a certain degree of subjugation." This is not to say, Your Honours, that there was no arming by Muslims or Croats, but instead that the Bosnian Serbs prepared themselves not to defend against Muslim physical aggression but to implement their objectives by force after the loss of the political battle. As for desiring peace, Bosnian Serb leaders, Mr. Krajisnik in particular, were not prepared to accept the political defeat represented by an independent Bosnia. In his remarks that were taped at the 28 February Deputies Club, after telling deputies that the Muslims wanted an Islamic state, Mr. Krajisnik told the deputies that would not happen. Instead, he and other leaders would come to them and say, he assured them: "Gentlemen, get your woolen socks ready, we are going to defend ourselves." Similar references by Mr. Krajisnik are found in the brief, with references to going for "what we have done for centuries - win our own territories by force," or "you know what our profession has always been, to wage war." That's at the 8th Assembly, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik asks the Court to ignore the plain meaning of these words, asserting, instead, that he was trying to dissuade the deputies by reminding them of the tragic consequences of war. This assertion is wholly misleading. A recurring theme throughout the Assemblies is the Serbs were always victorious in war but somehow lost the peace. And as we've seen, this time Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic did their utmost to ensure that the gains of war would not be lost. The Defence assertion that Bosnian Serb leaders intended merely to "retain" territory echoes Mr. Krajisnik's testimony that the Bosnian Serbs sought only areas in which they were already a majority, as reflected by the maps presented by Serbs, he asserted, during the Cutileiro discussions. That was false. First, Mr. Krajisnik himself conceded during testimony that "it was impossible to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina in clearly divided ethnic territories, areas where one ethnic community would be a clear majority." Put another way, in the context of Serb territorial aspirations, it was impossible to ethnically divide Bosnia except by force, as Ambassador Okun and other international witnesses have explained. Indeed, the negotiations that Mr. Krajisnik talked about so fulsomely did not identify the extent of Bosnian Serb territorial ambitions. On the 18th of March at the Assembly, when a deputy complained that Prijedor was not included as Serb territory on the map he was shown, Mr. Krajisnik quickly reassured him: "Please, let us not take the maps seriously." Recall also, Your Honours, that Mr. Krajisnik falsely asserted that a map of territorial division was part of the 18 March agreement in principle, stemming from the Cutileiro discussions, despite the fact that the agreement explicitly attached only a map depicting the existing municipalities and the existing demographic breakdown in those municipalities. The negotiations were simply part of a process for the Bosnian Serbs. While the ultimate goals must remain secret, Dr. Karadzic told deputies at that same session, when the attention of the world is no longer on them, everything will be possible, even changing the borders. Meanwhile, their goal, he said, was to make the internal borders as wide as possible. And once negotiations had broken down and the conflict was under way, this incremental approach was no longer advantageous and Bosnian Serb territorial aspirations could be, and were, directly pursued. The Drina region, for example, to ensure that there was no border between the Bosnian Serb state and Serbia and which would be, in Mr. Krajisnik's own words in the Srpsko Oslobodjenje interview, the backbone of the Serbian people. Also the corridor connecting Krajina to Semberija, the territory to the Una, and the rest of the territorial ambitions reflected in the strategic objectives. These, Your Honours, were not territories retained but, in the repeated words of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders "liberated" or "conquered." As Dr. Karadzic said at the 17th Assembly in July 1992: "We have liberated almost everything that is ours." Or as Mr. Krajisnik said at the 36th Assembly: "At the beginning of the war Serbs marshalled their forces for the 'liberation of Serbian ethnic spaces.'" Your Honours, contrary to the map that was shown by Mr. Krajisnik during his testimony, with the Serbs seeking only this modest area reflected by the red line which weaves its way carefully through predominantly Muslim-populated areas, let me show you a map which reveals the extent of Serb conquest. That's a map we've seen in court through the course of Mr. Krajisnik speaking on a video. This map, Your Honour, reflects the territories that had been conquered or liberated by Serbian forces. Let me show you another map before I go on to Mr. Krajisnik's remarks at that time. That's a map of the -- this is a better picture of that map, and let me show you quickly a map of the municipalities involved. Especially look at the Eastern Bosnia region. These are some of the municipalities, Your Honour, that are involved, and you can see the demographic breakdown in those municipalities, including the ones in Bratunac, Srebrenica, Visegrad, Rogatica, Zvornik, Vlasenica, and so on. And yet when Mr. Krajisnik explained the video map to the Serbian public on television, he said: "I can only say that what was being said, that we are possessing the territories ethnically populated by the other national communities, that is not true." And his remarks were technically correct because the Muslims were no longer there. As Dr. Karadzic explained at the 53rd Session with regard to those same municipalities: "There are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves and there were only 30 per cent of us ..." And he went on: "Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance, they had to become ours, and no one is practically questioning it any more." As Dr. Karadzic explained to the deputies on the 28th of February, this was fundamentally an ethnic conflict of the sort that necessitates re-settlement, and then he stated: "Muslims cannot live with others. We must be clear on that." As Defence Witness Kasagic acknowledged, that meant that the Muslim population had to be reduced to a certain percentage, recalling the figure of 5 per cent. And after Dr. Karadzic had told the deputies that Muslims couldn't live with others, Mr. Krajisnik then told them: "I tell you, everything we do in this parliament, everything I do personally, I do exclusively for pure areas." These pure areas, Your Honours, were not created by some theoretical inevitability of wartime population movements; they were the result of military efforts by the Bosnian Serb forces. Thus, when Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic went to negotiations to demand that these newly Serb territories be kept by Republika Srpska, Mladic could say proudly to the Assembly, as he did: "I have to say to our delegation, which I really appreciate together with our president, Mr. President, you have started from the most favourable starting position in Geneva. You had the military result in your hands." Your Honours, let me next turn, if I may, to the issue of leadership. The ethnic division of Bosnia by force required concerted action. The Bosnian Serb leadership, as detailed in the brief, assembled the bodies and forces necessary to accomplish that: Assemblies, Crisis Staffs, Council of Ministers, police, government, Presidency, NSC, army, et cetera. These organs were part of a hierarchical structure which implemented the policy of forcible ethnic separation. At the top of this leadership structure throughout, in positions of formal authority which mirrored their de facto power, were Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic. Now, in the early phases of this case, the Defence disputed that Mr. Krajisnik was a leader. That position yielded to mounting evidence of Mr. Krajisnik's involvement at the highest levels of everything that went on within the Bosnian Serb leadership structure. Now the Defence acknowledges that Mr. Krajisnik was a leader but asserts that he was not a controlling figure because the expanded Presidency did not exist, the National Security Council was not a legal body, and that his other positions were of insufficient significance to render him criminally liable. Let me turn first to the expanded or War Presidency. There has never been a dispute that a formal declaration of war was not declared. That fact, however, does not control the determination that this body was a source of de jure control. As the Defence brief itself acknowledges, de jure control refers to power derived from appointed positions. It is not, Your Honours, concerned with whether there was a technical legal deficiency in that position. And there is abundant evidence that the War Presidency or expanded Presidency existed. First, the records of the expanded Presidency themselves demonstrate its existence and Mr. Krajisnik's membership in it. He is referred to repeatedly as member, he signed Presidency documents, chaired a session, and was allocated Presidency responsibilities. The Presidency decision on the formation of war commissions of June 10th, 1992, makes three explicit references to "the War Presidency of the Republic." Your Honours, if I may, I'd like to move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Defence also asserts, Your Honours, that the unreliability of the minutes is reflected in the listing of Trbojevic as a member of the Presidency in the minutes of the 27th Session. That assertion, however, is grounded on an incorrect translation, which was corrected in court during Mr. Treanor's testimony, and the correct translation distinguishes Trbojevic from the other members of the Presidency, including Mr. Krajisnik. More importantly, Your Honours, the Defence brief ignores the contemporaneous references to the existence of the war or expanded Presidency, including references by top officials Maksimovic, Djokanovic, Subotic, Trbojevic, implicit references by both Dr. Karadzic and Krajisnik, the lengthy debate at the Assembly about the "existence" of the expanded Presidency, and ignores the expanded Presidency's own inquiry into whether RS should "stick with" that body, as well as the testimony of Trbojevic and Djokanovic and the testimony of former Presidency members, Djeric and Plavsic. The Defence contends that Djeric did not say that the War Presidency existed or that he was a member and testified that it did not actually function. In fact, Mr. Djeric said explicitly that Mr. Krajisnik "was a member of the Presidency by virtue of his office as Speaker of the Parliament, so that is how he was a member of that body, just like I was there as Prime Minister." And Djeric also made clear what he meant by his comment that the Presidency didn't function. First, he noted that he thought Plavsic or Koljevic should have chaired the meetings; and second, he testified that Mr. Krajisnik never disagreed with Dr. Karadzic and in most cases Koljevic would take "their side, the side of those two." Therefore, in most cases "there was no need for a vote." Mrs. Plavsic had essentially the same complaint about the way the expanded Presidency functioned: "I said many times that the Presidency, which did not function properly, was only a waste of money and that two persons, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, decided everything." The Defence assertion that Mrs. Plavsic did not provide any useful evidence concerning the existence of the expanded Presidency or the nature of the meetings is quite erroneous. Beyond the excerpt from her statement just cited, in her statement she directed the Court to sections of her book that she considered relevant to Mr. Krajisnik. In court she testified that, "I wrote there that the name of the book is very binding, as far as I'm concerned. That's why I called the book 'I Testify.' And I said it as if I had given an oath that I would speak the truth, only the truth, so help me God. And that's what also kept, like a thread, appearing throughout this book and also the second book." And here is what she wrote: "Who was the expanded Presidency? Members of the Presidency elected to the Assembly on 12 May 1992, the Assembly president, and the Prime Minister." And she explained that the expanded Presidency existed until December, when it gave way to a single president; Mr. Karadzic. This body, Your Honours, was the supreme commander of the army and empowered to issue orders to the police and exercise control over municipal authorities. Quickly explained, Article 174 of the law on the army provides that the president is the supreme commander; amendments to Article 5 of the constitutional law for the implementation of the constitution on the 12th of May and the 1st of June vested those duties in the Presidency and then the expanded Presidency, as explained in detail in P64, paragraphs 260 through 264. As Main Staff member Gvero stated at the 19th Assembly: "Shortly the basic elements are: There is the Supreme Command of the army, and that is the president of the republic as the supreme commander. In our situation, this will be the Presidency. All the elements of defence and the army are subordinated to this institution. We, in the army, are following this and are trying to fully observe it. There was no significant act that was passed without this in mind." Your Honours, the National Security Council, the NSC, and the three-member collective Presidency preceded the five-member War Presidency. The NSC, was chaired by Dr. Karadzic and took the important executive decisions in that period, which were then formalised through the acting presidents, one of whom, Mrs. Plavsic, was in Sarajevo, or the Assembly. Now, similar to its technical attack on the so-called legality of the War Presidency, the Defence claims that the NSC was not a legal body. This is an assertion that ignores the evidence of its establishment by the Assembly, the formal records of its existence and its decisions, the testimony of witnesses who did not suggest that it was illegal or did not exist, and Mr. Krajisnik's own acknowledgement that it functioned, referring to the introduction of the state of imminent threat of war, he acknowledged, "The discussion here -" referring to the minutes of the NSC meeting - "indicate that it was the council that proposed that." Now, quickly, Your Honour, before moving on, I wanted to address question 9 the Court posed to the parties regarding the body known as the -- well, there's a question about the Supreme Defence Council. I don't believe there's any dispute among the parties that there was no body in RS by that name, but instead only a body that was titled "Supreme Command." That body was formed after the debate about whether or not the expanded Presidency should continue in late November, and thereafter Dr. Karadzic became the single president and the Supreme Command was formed. Mrs. Plavsic's use of the term "Supreme Defence Council," based on an examination of the transcript, appears to reflect simple confusion between the Supreme Command in Republika Srpska and a similar body called the Supreme Defence Council in Serbia and Montenegro. And you can see that confusion beginning in her transcript references when she tries to recall the name of the body and says it's like the body in Serbia and Montenegro. As far as her reference to a meeting of that body in June, that's either a simple misrecollection of date or a reflection of some meeting, an ad hoc meeting of similar persons who comprised the membership of the Supreme Command at a later time. Your Honours, I'd like to move past the discussion of the formal bodies and note this: Beyond Mr. Krajisnik's membership on these formal bodies, it is more important to recall that these structures were both a reflection of his power as well as the source of it. As Trbojevic testified, suggested the establishment of the expanded Presidency did not change the division of power, but rather formalised it. The evidence from witness after witness revealed the duumvirate of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Dr. Karadzic, who was openly heralded as the undisputed leader of the Bosnian Serbs, and Mr. Krajisnik, his trusted, organised, meticulous, complement and a formidable power in his own right. As we heard, people were considered either Radovan's man or Momo's man. When asked which he was, Mandic told us that he was "close to Momcilo Krajisnik." And later he explained the nature of that subordinate relationship by saying: "You know how subordination and superiority in the government functions." And he provided us with an example referring to a Muslim whom Mr. Krajisnik wanted released from detention. Mandic told us: "I carried out this order. I acted as a soldier carrying out his order. If I found the man there, I would ask the army to release him or if -- or the police who were holding them. I would tell them that Mr. Krajisnik had ordered me to bring this man to Vrbanja and that he be released to go back to Sarajevo. And I would personally escort this person and then inform Mr. Krajisnik that I had carried out his instruction." Trbojevic knew that he could not become Deputy Prime Minister without the approval of both Karadzic and Krajisnik, and it was "crystal clear" to Prstojevic that Karadzic and Krajisnik could remove any municipal official. The many intercepted telephone calls reveal that relationship and reveal a pair taking decisions, formulating policy, selecting personnel, calling others to meetings, praising each other, disparaging others in a manner reflecting their mutually superior rank. Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were a very effective team. In addition to their positions together on the top executive bodies, Mr. Krajisnik was the powerful president of the Assembly. From witnesses such as Trbojevic, Mandic, Neskovic, and Radic, we heard about Mr. Krajisnik's power over deputies and their derivative power in the municipalities. As one of the deputies noted at the February 28th Deputies' Club in comparing Mr. Krajisnik's mastery of the Assembly to a regional Assembly president: "The president of the Assembly -" that's Mr. Krajisnik - "has shown that he has to control the Assembly." Excuse me: "... has shown that he has to control the Assembly. Mr. Kupresanin, likewise, has to control the situation in Banja Luka." And thus, when a crisis hit, the president of the ARK Assembly, Kupresanin, urged "the president of the party and the president of the Assembly to come to Banja Luka and I am sure that nothing bad will happen." And that was at the 8th Assembly. Beyond its formal functions, the Assembly was a neurocentre. Deputies were expected to disseminate policy to their municipalities, where they sat on Crisis Staffs, and to report back on what was happening in the field, and Mr. Krajisnik's office, as we heard, was constantly filled with deputies and municipal representatives. Thus, with their hands on the levers of power, Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic directed the effort to forcibly create an ethnically separate entity. Your Honours, one of the other issues, factual issues, in dispute based on the reading of the briefs concerns detention facilities. Now, detention facilities, the Prosecution has shown, were part of an extensive system. An extensive system of detention and exchange which was instituted and implemented under the direction of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Many thousands of non-Serb civilians were rounded up, held in brutal and inhumane conditions, and either killed or sent outside RS territory. The Defence asserts that evidence of Krajisnik's power -- or knowledge of detention facilities is "very patchy" and places great reliance on what it terms "the clear and succinct answers given by Mr. Krajisnik," which are also termed "clear and forthright." And during the course of his testimony Mr. Krajisnik said that he didn't know anything about camps until July or August 1992, when strict instructions were given to investigate. He suggested that the camps were secret and not known to the MUP, and he claimed that he would never countenance the detention of civilians, as reflected, among other things, by his assertions that he was never at a meeting where measures were not taken in response to information about possible misconduct. Your Honours, one of the pervasive aspects of the pattern that we saw in this case, beginning with the imposition of increasingly restrictive measures on non-Serbs and loss of rights, and ending with massacres, was the establishment of detention facilities where civilians were held in inhumane conditions and where brutality varied only in degree. Like the forcible displacement of Muslims and Croats, the existence of such facilities in municipality after municipality was sufficient by itself to demonstrate a pattern too uniform to be ad hoc, but instead one that must be the product of a guiding hand above the municipalities. That inescapable conclusion is only buttressed by the fact that camps were set up and run by the army, police, and Crisis Staffs, all with their chains of communication and command up to the Presidency and, more particularly, to Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. The detention of civilians was systemic. Officials at all levels knew about the camps and a republic exchange system was established from the earliest stage to monitor and control the possible release of civilians. On the 24th of April, 1992, the NSC decided that the exchange of prisoners would be handled by the Ministry of Justice after internal affairs organs did their work. Now, these were civilian prisoners as well as so-called military prisoners, as we know from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please slow down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- the Dr. Djeric, 28 April -- [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem in switches. Please continue, Mr. Tieger -- no, please proceed and do not continue this speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, two weeks after the NSC decision that the exchange of prisoners would be handled by the Ministry of Justice after the police finished their work, the Ministry of Justice established a central commission for exchange of prisoners, a body which extended to the municipalities and regions and to the corps level of the army, and which prohibited the release of detainees without its order. That commission began functioning almost immediately. You will recall the 400 battered Muslims from Bratunac who, as Mr. Tupajic told us, were only a small part of the forcible expulsion of Muslims from Eastern Bosnia, who were on a list signed off by Markovic, the MUP member of the exchange commission. You will also recall that Prime Minister Dr. Djeric coordinated the effort, arranging for trucks from Crisis Staffs to transport those detainees. Mrs. Plavsic explained to General Wilson that the detention of people of military age was a pre-emptive action so that they would not participate in fighting. And that is borne out by the 6 June order of the exchange commission, the testimony of Mandic, and the accused himself, who testified that "the general opinion that prevailed was this, that the entire population and all the people, all the -- were actually the army, all ethnic groups with the army." Your Honours, let me show you an order from VRS Major Andric in Eastern Bosnia that also reflects precisely that, that the moving out is to be arranged, and men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange. In Western Bosnia, as well, thousands of Muslims were rounded up by the army and police and camps were established in Omarska and Trnopolje and other places, pursuant to a decision by the Crisis Staff. As Bosnian Serb conquests increased, however, conquests of Muslim areas, the camps filled and overcrowding became a security problem. On the 12th of June, 1992, General Mladic ordered the establishment of camps at the corps level in response. Batkovic was one of those camps. Manjaca, which was another corps-level camp, was already in operation by that time, receiving Muslims and Croats from the Crisis Staffs. Now, it was already in late May that the international community was concerned and expressed concern about the detention of Muslim and Croat civilians. On the 24th of May, concerned about the threat of air-strikes by the international community, Dr. Djeric wrote a letter to the United States Secretary of State denying the existence of camps. Ambassador Okun also testified about the international community's concern about camps and about knowledge of camps by June. On June 10th, 1992, the expanded Presidency, with Mr. Krajisnik, as always, present, after reviewing foreign press reports, decided that Djeric would have the government provide a report on detainees, and that day Djeric tasked the Ministry of Justice, which was in charge of the exchange commission, to make a report about prisoners, paying special attention to "treatment of civilian population." Now, that report was received five days later on June 15th, as we have seen more than once in this court. It generated a great deal of concern to a government already concerned about its public image. The issue of prisoners exchange, it wrote, is "extremely important, complex, and delicate." And if insufficient attention is paid, it can cause a number of negative consequences to the republic. A working group consisting of the very highest ranking members of government: The Prime Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister, the minister of justice, the minister of interior, the minister of defence, the minister of health, was formed to propose systemic solutions. But the oppressive system continued to operate. Recall the damning ICRC report about Manjaca, which was received by Dr. Karadzic and sent on to Dr. Djeric. Or the 17 July report of the minister of the interior to Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Djeric in which Stanisic reported that "the army, Crisis Staffs, and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible," noting that they were held in poor and dangerous conditions and requesting only clarification on who had jurisdiction over them. In addition, as we heard about Susica, efforts were made to hide prisoners. However, in the same way that Mr. Krajisnik and the Bosnian Serbs blame the Muslim political drive for independence for forcing them to conquer and cleanse the parts of Bosnia to which they felt entitled, the Bosnian Serbs blame the terrible conditions in camps on Muslims, asserting that their refusal to engage in exchanges of population were responsible. Incredibly, on 7 August, 1992, after the discovery of Omarska, Dr. Djeric issued a press release explaining that conditions in Omarska were bad because the other side doesn't want to exchange. Mr. Krajisnik, in fact, suggested the same in court, asserting that the fact that Muslims failed to implement a proposed all-for-all exchanges was a big mistake and many remained in prison where they were subjected to abuse and grave consequences. It is true, Your Honours, that both the Muslim authorities and the international community saw the exchange process precisely for what it was, a way to ethnically cleanse RS territory of Muslims. We heard that from Ambassador Okun and from other international witnesses - you will also recall the Mazowiecki report - and we also saw that from the 20th June, 1992, session of the Bosnian government, in which it was said, "If we don't accept the ultimatum, these people could be really hurt. If we accept it, we are legalising ethnic division, that is, the alteration of the demographic picture of Bosnia, the creation of ethnically clean territories like some precondition for the creation of some kind of Serbian state in BH." Indeed, Mr. Mandic told Mr. Krajisnik directly on 26 June 1992 that Filip Vukovic, who had a Serb name and was the head of the Muslim exchange commission, had made just that charge. Mr. Krajisnik's response was simply to call the man a "traitor." Mr. Krajisnik asserted in testimony that he did so because Mandic told him that the charge was false, but when asked to identify the portion of the conversation where Mandic denied that it was true, Mr. Krajisnik could only point to Mandic saying about Vukovic: "Fuck his mother." There was only one proper solution: The immediate release back to their homes, the solution that was expressly set out in Vukovic's facsimile and it was ignored. As for Mr. Krajisnik's repeated assertions that he and the rest of the Bosnian Serb leadership acted vigorously to "take measures urgently to punish perpetrators," because "if you wouldn't be interested in this kind of thing, then you would be committing a crime." They are belied, Your Honours, by the sham investigations in the wake of the Omarska outcry on the 5th of August, 1992. The Assembly never discussed the issue of prisoners, despite requests by deputies to do so. Mr. Krajisnik was asked by His Honour Judge Hanoteau whether he could have taken an initiate as president of the Assembly concerning the prisoners. Mr. Krajisnik told the Court that it was for the government to complete its investigation and submit a report to the Assembly. But the report's pretextual nature is clear. Even Mr. Krajisnik had to acknowledge the patent inadequacy of the August report on Eastern Bosnia camps. And in the end Mr. Krajisnik admitted he simply never read them. Your Honours, I'd also like to address one additional issue, factual issue, in dispute, and that is the issue of the Variant A and B document. I will be turning the floor over to Mr. Harmon. He will be talking, among other things, Crisis Staffs which flow from that document. We heard a great deal of testimony about that. As the Prosecution asserted at the beginning of the case and as it established, having decided to achieve a Serbian entity by force, the Bosnian Serb leadership began to put into place the necessary bodies and forces. Variant A and B, which is dated 19 December, 1991, as we all know, and which was disseminated immediately after, was an important clandestine outline to establish the municipal structures, particularly Crisis Staffs, and prepare for the take-over of power. The Defence minimises the significance of the instructions, asserting that there is little evidence of it being adopted or implemented. Well, Your Honours, although the Defence may attempt to minimise its significance, we can find a more accurate reflection of the significance in the remarks of Dr. Karadzic, as he said at the 46th Session: "Please, remember how we used to work before the war? Everything was as clear as day in the municipalities where we were a majority and in those where we were in minority. Do you remember the instruction A and instruction B? We had Crisis Staffs and it was clear they were the authority. They could make mistakes, but they were still the authority." And he reminisced again at the 50th Assembly: "At the moment the war began in the municipalities where we were in the majority, we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where we were in the minority, we set up secret government, municipal boards, Municipal Assemblies, presidents of Executive Boards. You will remember the A and B variants." Dr. Karadzic knew full well the role that Variant A and B had played in the run-up to the forcible take-over. As for the Defence assertion that there is little evidence of it being adopted or implemented, that completely ignores the evidence in this case. To the contrary, we have seen and heard evidence of Variant A and B being adopted in the following 23 places, 23: Banja Luka, Bihac, Bijeljina, Bratunac, Bosanska Krupa, Bosanski Brod, Bosanski Novi, Bosanski Petrovac, Centar Sarajevo, Donji Vakuf, Foca, Gorazde, Ilidza, Kljuc, Livno, Novo Sarajevo, Prijedor, Rogatica, Sarajevo City, Sokolac, Trnovo, Tuzla, and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Tieger, may I try to clarify one matter. May I take you to page 27, line 10 and 11. I thought as a matter of fact that you were referring also to Mr. Krajisnik and not only to Mr. Djeric who issued a press release. And the line abuse and consequences was used by Mr. Krajisnik, although not literally, and he says - how should I put it? - on the 15th of May during his examination-in-chief, and a question was put to him on the 14th of June in cross-examination. Were you just referring in these lines to the press release of Mr. Djeric or did you include in any way Mr. Krajisnik, which I thought I heard but might be wrong, but I don't -- I do not see it reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, let me clarify, and I appreciate the opportunity. Dr. Djeric issued the press release --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- on the 7th of August. I indicated that Mr. Krajisnik suggested essentially the same rationale in his testimony in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is that the failure to engage in exchange was the cause of the continued detention of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please look at page 27, lines 8 to 11, and see whether it reflects what you said, or otherwise we could check it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It does not, Your Honour, and I appreciate you recalling my attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, for clarification, the point was that on August 7th Dr. Djeric issued a press release explaining that conditions at Omarska were bad because the otherwise didn't want to exchange. I then went on to say that Mr. Krajisnik suggested essentially the same thing in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard. We'll check the correctness of the transcript in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just recited the number of municipalities for which we have evidence of the adoption of Variant A and B, receipt and adoption of A and B, and Dr. Karadzic's emphasis on its significance. From the beginning, Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik shepherded its implementation. They discussed it immediately after its dissemination, pondering who would implement it. The council of ministers or Mr. Cizmovic, who was the regional coordinator, and to whom Karadzic spoke that same day, agreeing both that Cizmovic would visit the municipalities and on the importance of the "realisation" of "those papers." By the 16th of January, Cizmovic had reported back to Karadzic on his visits to various municipalities and the extent of their preparation to "implement the first level of instructions." Cizmovic, who considered his position to be the third highest in Republika Srpska, reported to Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik about his work. At the 26th of January Assembly session, the 6th Session, which was called as an extraordinary session after further Muslim moves toward independence, Cizmovic observed that the Bosnian Serbs therefore had to solve or to deal with that pending issue through the establishment of their state, and he asserted "tasks set out in the instructions of 19 December 1991 should be carried out." A little more than two weeks later, at a meeting of SDS and Main Board and Executive Board and municipal leaders, Karadzic activated the second level of A and B in order to "intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory." At the Assembly session of the next day it was proposed that Cizmovic tour all municipalities to determine whether they were prepared to be operational and "exercise power over the territory that is ours." Karadzic proposed that a checklist and reminder be prepared for the municipalities and suggested therefore that "we should meet later in Mr. Krajisnik's conference's room." And by March 18th, 1992, the Assembly session at which Mr. Krajisnik told the deputies that it would be good to start implementing the ethnic division on the ground, Karadzic reminded deputies that the foundations were nearly in place and "it is up to you to decide when we will reveal our next move. It will all be happening in a flash and the set-up of the de facto situation based on our documents." Your Honour, at this point, I'd like to yield the floor to Mr. Harmon who will address further factual issues in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, another issue of fact that's in dispute is whether Mr. Krajisnik had knowledge of the crimes that are described in the indictment as being committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. His position is set out in paragraph 206 of the Defence brief, where it's asserted that: "Mr. Krajisnik has always emphatically denied any knowledge of the crimes charged. In the fog of war the truth can be hard to discern and he was entitled to be skeptical of any reports received, to question and to seek verification as to its truth." Now, what type of crimes are we talking about in 1992 about which he claims he had no knowledge? Expulsions, deportations, killings, detentions of civilians, camps with dreadfully poor conditions, destruction of sacred sites, looting, destruction of non-Serb villages, homes. I dare say, if Mr. Krajisnik is believed, that he may have been the only person living in Bosnia who was unaware of what was happening in his country. In response to one of Judge Canivell's questions, he asserted that he got information but that the media was reporting things that he knew were not true; that he had the impression that everything was rigged and that everything was false. Now, the Defence asserts the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Krajisnik did receive actual and verified reports indicating that crimes were being or were about to be committed. And I want to focus the Court's attention on some of the evidence that demonstrates that in 1992 Mr. Krajisnik received verified reports of the types of crimes that are described in the indictment. I'll focus first, if I can, Your Honour, on the internal Bosnian Serb sources of information. The first event that happened in Bosnia was Bijeljina, and that was a dramatic event that gripped the nation. A presidential commission which included Mrs. Plavsic was sent to Bijeljina. And as Mr. Kljuic testified, Mr. Krajisnik received police reports about what had happened there. I think Mr. Kljuic's words were: He knew more than us. On May the 9th, 1992, the village of Glogova was razed to the ground. The decision to destroy the village and ethnically cleanse it was sanctioned by authorities at the republican level - Assemblyman Zekic - and by Serbian state authorities from the security service. It was the Crisis Staff who formulated and took a formal decision to attack the village, expel its population, burn the village to the ground, and to continue those types of actions against other villages in the Bratunac municipality. The following day, members of the -- what we allege were members of the joint criminal enterprise participated in that attack, members of the Crisis Staff, the JNA, the Territorial Defence, the police, and volunteers from Serbia. They leveled the village, they killed 65 of Muslim inhabitants from that village, and they expelled the survivors and burned the village. Two days later, on or about the 11th of May, 1992, Mr. Deronjic was summoned to a meeting in Pale where he and other Crisis Staff members convened in the presence of General Mladic, Radovan Karadzic, and Velibor Ostojic. Those were the people who were directing the meeting. And they sat at a podium in front of maps. Mr. Deronjic described to the Serbian leaders, the Bosnian Serbian leaders, what exactly he had done and how those offensive operations were continuing and going to continue in Bratunac. He received applause from the other municipal persons, municipal Crisis Staff presidents, and Mr. Ostojic commented: "Now the municipality can be painted blue." Two days later Mr. Krajisnik, at the 16th Assembly Session, said: "I like Ostojic's blue maps." It's our submission, Your Honour, that Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Karadzic informed Mr. Krajisnik about the events in Glogova. Furthermore, between the 14th and the 17th of May, 400 men ethnically cleansed from Bratunac arrived in Pale. You heard the evidence of Sulejman Crncalo, who was a Muslim from Pale. He testified that he was with the president of the Serbian municipality of Pale, a man by the name of Starcevic, and together they observed the 400 men, many of whom had visible signs of beatings. Mr. Krajisnik himself testified that he learned that Deronjic had sent the Muslims to Pale, and he also testified that he met with Mr. Starcevic and discussed the 400 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I'm going to just interrupt you on the last line. On footnote 1056 you say this information is the testimony of Mr. Deronjic, but exactly the same information in footnote 1137 you say it's the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik, which is a bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll clarify that, yes, Your Honour. What I say, Your Honour, is that the information about what happened to the people in Glogova was reported in a meeting in Pale that Mr. Deronjic had been directed to attend. There he made -- there he related precisely what had happened to the Muslims -- the Muslim community in Bratunac. As I say -- if there's some confusion in the footnotes, I'll take a look at them and I'll address that after the first break. It may be an error, Your Honour. But let me return to the types of notice that Mr. Krajisnik had. You heard the testimony of Mr. Divcic, who said that the arrival of the 400 Muslims was the talk of the town. There's no doubt that Mr. Krajisnik was informed about the 400 Muslims who had been ethnically cleansed from Bratunac and about whom Mr. Deronjic had reported only a few days earlier. Mr. Krajisnik also was informed directly that the village of Misoca, a Muslim settlement, had been cleansed. That's found in an intercept that's identified in the evidence. The village of Ahatovici, where there was a massacre. Mr. Krajisnik was informed by his brother about the events relating to a massacre at Ahatovici. I'll be going later into private session to discuss Mr. Krajisnik's knowledge about a massive bombardment that occurred in Sarajevo. I won't do so now, I'm merely foreshadowing that as another point of reference for the types of evidence that showed Mr. Krajisnik was fully aware of what was happening in Bosnia. Also, Your Honour, if we examine the evidence of Mr. Dragan Djokanovic, who was a war commissioner. He testified that on the 16th and 17th of June he informed Mr. Krajisnik and members of the Presidency that serious crimes had been perpetrated in Zvornik. On the 17th of July, as well, the same day the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic, addressed a report to the president of the Presidency in which he informed: "The army, Crisis Staffs, and War Presidency have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians ..." And it described the conditions in the camps as being quite poor and not observing international norms. Mrs. Plavsic testified about the notorious criminal Batko. She said she brought his conduct to the attention of Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Mandic, and others, and they were indifferent. Mr. Kasagic confirmed that he had learned of the forcible expulsion of Muslims and Croats at Assembly sessions and that all Assembly members were aware of that. Mr. Karadzic was repeatedly informed about crimes committed in Bosnia, and given his close relationship with Mr. Krajisnik, it's unimaginable that the subject of such crimes was not discussed in their daily intercourse. Finally, Mr. Krajisnik had the opportunity to travel through Bosnia, and he could see first-hand the results of the ethnic cleansing that had occurred in 1992. Now, if we also look, Your Honour, at external sources of information, let me recall the testimony of a witness from an international organisation who gave direct and specific information to Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Koljevic, and Mr. Karadzic about ethnic cleansing in Zvornik. Mr. Okun testified that frequent and repeated complaints were made at international negotiations to Krajisnik and others about the types of crimes that are at issue here and that those crimes were not denied. The ICRC made reports directly to Mr. Krajisnik and others. The media to which Mr. Krajisnik had access, we heard that from Mr. Ostojic, contained reports of these crimes. Tadeusz Mazowiecki, the former Prime Minister of Poland, prepared four reports for the United Nations in which he described the crimes committed by all parties. He described ethnic cleansing. He described the features and particular characteristics of ethnic cleansing and what it meant in real terms. It's interesting to note that Mr. Krajisnik, as we know from the evidence, said that Mr. Mazowiecki was bribed, his reports were not credible and honest. And yet Mr. Mazowiecki's reports, in many respects, contain the same identification that Mr. Stanisic's report contained, the report of the 17th of July, that civilians were being rounded up, that they were in camp, that the conditions were in contravention of legal standards. The bottom line, Your Honour, is that Mr. Krajisnik's assertion that he did not -- that it was hard to be -- that it was difficult, I should say, to discern what is true is, in fact, correct if your eyes are closed and your ears are closed and you're at the heart of a criminal enterprise. But it's our submission, Your Honour, that Mr. Krajisnik did receive reports, credible verified reports about ethnic cleansing, and when he testified that he did not, he was untruthful. Now, I'd like to turn to the issue of Crisis Staffs because that's another issue that's raised in the Defence brief. In paragraph 408 of the Defence brief, the Defence asserts that there is extreme patchiness in respect of when Crisis Staffs existed, and even sometimes whether they existed, how long they existed, their membership and authority, their actions, their independence or autonomy, and their involvement in criminal acts on the ground. I want to address these issues. But, by my calculation, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber has received evidence of Crisis Staffs in virtually all of the indictment municipalities, as well as evidence about War Presidencies in another four municipalities. Your Honour, could I find out when we're going to take the break? I'm prepared to continue. I just don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are now, I think, one hour and 25 minutes approximately, so we usually have the first break after one and a half hours. So you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll take my five minutes, Your Honour. Thank you. In its brief the Defence makes a number of assertions. First of all, it asserts that Crisis Staffs were casual, spontaneous bodies; that these bodies were created at people in the municipality's own initiative. And, according to Mr. Krajisnik, establishing a Crisis Staff was just like saying good morning. The second issue that is addressed in the brief is that, bearing in mind the casual nature of the Crisis Staffs, it's simply irrational to believe that Krajisnik had knowledge about and was informed what the Crisis Staffs were doing. The third issue is that there is nothing to demonstrate any significant contact or control by Mr. Krajisnik relating to municipal Crisis Staffs. And four, the fourth issue, is that there was extreme patchiness in the evidence about the Crisis Staff's involvement in criminal acts on the ground. Let me take the first issue, the first issue being that Crisis Staffs were casual and spontaneous bodies. Crisis Staffs may have been casual, ad hoc bodies under the communist system, but the Crisis Staffs that concern us in this trial and that we've been talking about for over two years were deliberately established by the Bosnian Serb leadership through Variant A and B as preparations for the take-over of power. Our evidence shows that Crisis Staffs declared themselves to be the sole municipal authority on the ground, taking all the prerogatives of the Municipal Assembly. We know from Mr. Djeric's instructions on the work of Crisis Staffs that were promulgated on the 26th of April, Crisis Staffs were explicitly stated to take over all the prerogatives and functions of Municipal Assemblies when they are not able to convene. Likewise, the Presidency decision on the formation of War Presidencies from the 31st of May stated that War Presidencies were to carry out all functions of the Assembly and executive organs as well as the work of state organs. Now, we have presented through the course of this trial countless examples of Crisis Staffs replacing Municipal Assemblies and asserting themselves to be the municipal authority. I direct Your Honours' attention to paragraph 40 of the report prepared by Ms. Hanson, but I'll give you some examples. Bosanski Samac, on the 30th of May, the Crisis Staff claimed the prerogatives of the Municipal Assembly. In Bratunac, the Crisis Staff took over from the Municipal Assembly. In Brcko, the War Assembly assumed all authorities of the Municipal Assembly. In Hadzici, "the Crisis Staff took over the complete authorities of the Municipal Assembly and its organs and services." In Ilidza, a 10th of May decision, 1992, the decision of the Crisis Staff "is to be regarded as a decision of the Serbian Assembly of the municipality of Ilidza." In Ilijas, the Crisis Staff assumed all the responsibilities of the government. I could go on, Your Honour. There are many more examples that are found in Ms. Hanson's report. I think this would be an appropriate time to break, Your Honour. I'm about to address the second issue raised by the Defence in its brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Since we had a late start, not due to ourselves, and since the Prosecution specifically asked to get all the time, we'll have a break until 20 minutes past 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, to begin, first of all, I've looked at the footnote 1056 and the name Krajisnik should be inserted in lieu of Deronjic. I had finished the issue of whether these were spontaneous bodies. It's our submission, Your Honour, that Crisis Staffs were planned and well-designed parts of the system created by the Serbs to ensure Bosnian Serb hegemony in the territories that they coveted. Now, the next point made in the Defence brief deals with the -- in fact, the Defence says it's irrational to believe that Krajisnik had knowledge about and was informed what the municipal Crisis Staffs were doing. We've presented considerable evidence to the contrary. First, the Crisis Staff reported to bodies which Mr. Krajisnik was a member, and Mr. Krajisnik had personal contacts with Crisis Staff presidents and knowledge of their actions. I just want to give you some examples; more are mentioned in the Hanson report. But on the 1st of April, 1992, the Bijeljina municipal Crisis Staff reported to the SDS Main Board on the situation as of 2000 hours, and this is precisely the period when Bijeljina was being taken over by the Bosnian Serb forces under the leadership of the Crisis Staff. That same day Mr. Krajisnik called the Bijeljina Crisis Staff and he talked to President Micic and he also talked to Mauzer, the paramilitary leader. On the 28th of April, 1992, the National Security Council minutes reflect that the National Security Council accepted a report on the work of the Crisis Staffs. Second, Mr. Krajisnik had information about the Crisis Staffs through the Presidency. Mr. Djeric's instructions instructed Crisis Staffs -- Mr. Djeric's instructions -- testimony, I'm sorry, was "those were the heads or, rather, chiefs of various Crisis Staffs of various entities of various municipalities, individually and so on and so forth." He went on to say: "I mean they had this party line primarily and they set store by that, and quite simply they would sideline the government and go directly to the Presidency." Radomir Neskovic, who was the president of the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff, described an occasion in June of 1992 when he and other Crisis Staff presidents were summoned to the Bistrik Hotel in Pale in order to report on their work. And Mr. Neskovic submitted a written report on their work to the president of the Presidency. Mr. Krajisnik also had knowledge of the work of the Crisis Staffs through the Assembly. Dragan Djukanovic testified to a case -- to this point. He said: "Most deputies in the People's Assembly were in their constituencies also members of Crisis Staffs and commissions. A large number of them were republican commissioners in the second half of 1992." When you examine the minutes of the Assembly, you'll notice that many of the people who were deputies and also involved in Crisis Staff work who -- representatives of Crisis Staff discussed what was happening in their municipalities. I refer to Trifko Radic from Ilijas, Miroslav Vjestica from Bosanska Krupa, and Milenko Vojinovic from Brcko. Mr. Krajisnik also had information about what was happening in Crisis Staffs and their activities through his personal contacts. On the 3rd of April, 1992, there's an intercept between Mr. Krajisnik and Jovan Tintor, the SDS Crisis Staff head from Vogosca. In that intercept, Mr. Krajisnik refers to Mr. Tintor as his kum. And Mr. Tintor says: "Please, it's my duty to inform you what's going on." In response to a question by Judge Hanoteau, Mr. Prstojevic, who was the president of the Ilidza Crisis Staff, testified: "As a native of Sarajevo, he, Krajisnik, had special concern for the Serbs of Sarajevo, and we could go to Mr. Krajisnik at any time. His door was always open to us. We could be received for an interview, we could call him on the telephone, and we could ask for help. We could ask him for his advice, and the president was able to either praise or criticise our work." On the 12th of May, 1992, Assembly session, Trifko Radic, who was the Crisis Staff president from Ilijas said that he released a prisoner: "On the intervention of the president of the Assembly," an example of Krajisnik's power over the Crisis Staff president. At the 20th Session, Mr. Radic said: "The Ustasha attack us on all fronts every day. We have no help. I went to see Mr. Krajisnik and General Mladic, and if they hadn't come, we would have fallen a long time ago." Finally Mr. Milan Tupajic, who was the president of the Crisis Staff from Sokolac, testified about his meetings with Mr. Krajisnik. He said: "I remember several working meetings with Mr. Krajisnik during which I was present. There was some more official meetings and there was also some chance encounters when they came to the municipality." Mr. Krajisnik also had knowledge and control, especially to the republican war commissioners. War Presidencies and war commissioners were established to replace Crisis Staffs and to tighten central control over municipal authorities by means of the republican war commissioner. They came into existence in April of 1992. Milan Tupajic, who I just referred to, said that war commissioners were a way for the members to gain insight into the developments in municipalities in order that they could inform the president of the Assembly and the president of the republic. He said that war commissioners were members of The National Assembly. "A certain number of member MPs were indeed appointed as war commissioners which in the last analysis is only logical, since they came from the base." Now, I earlier mentioned Mr. Dragan Djukanovic, who was a war commissioner and who reported directly to the Presidency. Mr. Djukanovic reported in -- about crimes that he had observed in Zvornik. "When I went back to Pale I informed Karadzic and Krajisnik of all the observations that I had made on my visits to the municipalities and all the events that I had learned. I performed my mandate to establish governments. I conveyed general information about the situation in the places I had visited to the War Presidency, informing them that many bad things had happened." Mr. Poplasen, a Defence witness, testified that the -- that he reported orally and in writing to the Presidency members, and one exhibit, a copy of a document dated the 24th of June, 1992, from war commissioner Poplasen addressed to the Serb Republic of BiH wartime Presidency reported that a prison in Vogosca was illegal. Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the Presidency and responsible for the work of war commissioners. Referring to their work of the 22nd Session, he said that their work was: "Very efficient and good. I know that every deputy from the Assembly who went, Mirko Mijatovic, Jovo Mijatovic, Cancar, Marko Simic, Branko Simic, Vojo Maksimovic, they all provided great service because they tried to resolve all problems when they arrived together with the people." The brief also notes that there's nothing to demonstrate any significant control by Krajisnik relating to municipal Crisis Staffs. There is no document in evidence reflecting that Krajisnik issued a direct order to the Crisis Staff. Crisis Staffs were part of the state system created to seize and to hold power. They operated under the authority and at the direction of state organs of which Krajisnik was a member. They were not rogue bodies implementing policies on their own. The evidence that we have presented shows that Crisis Staffs received and implemented orders from the republic level. Mr. Pasic, from Bosanski Novi, in response to a question I posed, said: "You asked me whether the Crisis Staff acted in accordance with these decisions of the Republika Srpska Assembly and other bodies and authorities. I have already mentioned in my testimony that the Crisis Staff had no choice and could not have undertaken anything else." We've also -- other documents have come into evidence; they're referred to in Ms. Hanson's report. Evidence has been adduced at these proceedings that Crisis Staff presidents reported directly to the Presidency and to Mr. Krajisnik and largely bypassed the government. I've mentioned two examples already; the example of Mr. Prstojevic and the testimony of former Prime Minister Djeric. And I've also mentioned the testimony of Mr. Neskovic, who was summoned to the Bistrik Hotel in Pale in order to report on the work of Presidency -- the work of Crisis Staffs. Lastly, let me address the assertion that there was extreme patchiness in the evidence about the Crisis Staffs involvement in criminal acts on the ground. To make it perfectly clear, it is our submission, Your Honour, that Crisis Staffs were not benign organisations; they were essential. In the persecutory campaign, they ordered and enforced discriminatory measures against Muslims and Croats, they implemented the forcible removal of non-Serbs and the systematic seizure of property of those persons who were forced out of those municipalities. I'm going to direct your attention briefly to some of that evidence that deals with their involvement in criminal acts on the ground. The 23rd July 1992 War Presidency decision from Celinac severely restricted the movement of Muslims who resided in the community. They couldn't linger on the streets, they couldn't sell or exchange property, they couldn't drive cars, they couldn't hunt, fish, or swim in rivers. I've described the attack on Glogova that was the result of a Crisis Staff decision. In late May of 1992, the Crisis Staff in Prijedor decided to establish detention centres at Trnopolje, Keraterm, and Omarska. At the end of May 1992, the Sanski Most Crisis Staff ordered the establishment of detention facilities at the sports hall Betonirka in Krings. In that same municipality, the Crisis Staff listed the type of persons who were undesirable in the municipality of Sanski Most: Politicians, nationalists, extremists, and people unwelcome in Sanski Most, and indeed sent many of those people to Manjaca where some perished en route and some perished in the camp. The Bosanski Petrovac Crisis Staff set up a prison in Kozila so that it could in its own words "arrest all military-capable people who could possibly harm the Serbs." In Bosanska Krupa, the War Presidency in its own words "suggested two options to the Muslims: Either to organise their own evacuation from the area or to have that effected by military means." And lastly, I refer Your Honours to the two documents, one of which is in 1993, Mr. Prstojevic from the Ilidza war commission forbade the return of all Muslims and Croats to his municipality. And the 7 June, 1992, decision of seven municipal Crisis Staff presidents who demanded that Muslims and Croats should move out of "our municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented. And if the leadership of the autonomous region of Krajina and Banja Luka fails to solve this issue, our seven municipalities will take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipality to the centre of Banja Luka." Those seven municipalities were Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpksa Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc. Now, Your Honours, let me turn to another issue in dispute; the strategic objectives. Mr. Tieger has addressed some of this. As we know, the strategic objectives were formally announced at the 16th Session. We know from that -- transcripts from that session, that strategic objective number 1, which was the establishment of state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities was the most important objective, according to Mr. Krajisnik, who said to both the assembled deputies and General Mladic and the assembled military persons: "The first goal is the most important one. And in relation to all other goals, all other goals are subsets of the first one." Now, these strategic objectives constituted the core political and military objectives of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Many witnesses who testified here noted the blinding reality that ethnic separation could not be achieved in Bosnia without the use of force. Now, Mr. Krajisnik testified that those objectives that were enunciated at the 16th Session were: "Political objectives only and were not intended to form part of the military planning that was to implement the programme of war being pursued by the army." In his testimony he insisted there was no link between the military objectives described in the army report and the strategic objectives enunciated at the 16th Session. Mr. Krajisnik, according to the evidence we have presented, had numerous contacts with General Mladic, members of his staff; Presidency session minutes reflect that. Our brief reflects those contacts at paragraphs 398 to 401. When Mr. Krajisnik was asked if he ever asked the military: What are your objectives? What are you trying to achieve? His answer was: I don't remember having asked such a question. That's an incredible answer, given the fact that the Serbs were fighting for their own survival against what they had publicly announced were the genocidal elements in the other ethnic groups and that they were fighting for their age-old dreams of establishing a Serb state. Can Your Honours imagine any wartime leader of any country not asking his or her military chiefs: What are your objectives? What are you trying to achieve? It's clear from looking at the 16th Assembly Session transcripts that the people who were present, the Assemblymen, understood these to be military objectives. Mr. Beli, and I quote: "These are the war goals that people must know they are to do at any moment."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Since I heard the proposer say it was our second strategic goal, please allow me in that case we must jointly work on furthering that interest in a military sense, too."

utterances.speaker: MR. RADIC
utterances.text: "As the president said, let us set our goals and tasks, see exactly what is ours and how much we should occupy and then divide up." He went on to say: "Please work on this and please give us our goals so that we know what we are going to take." Mr. Ostojic testified in respect of the strategic objectives: "We have the idea and the realisation of this map of ours, and I do believe I was the first to start drawing the map, but they are an idea on which the diplomacy has to work. They are -- they, the borders, will be drawn and established only when we make them a fact. I believe that peace with Alija can only be achieved by war."
