And lastly, Mr. Mijatovic said -- he asked "to give the floor to the experts in the military field so that they can tell us their vision and their overview, and I hope that we will all see much more clearly what the duties are facing us, what it is that we have to do to fulfil the six strategic goals we recently put before the Serbian people and the Serbian Republic of BH." Now, the evidence that these strategic goals were understood by the military are contained in our brief at pages 117 to 122. The army report makes it crystal clear. It says: "The strategic objectives were military -- the strategic objectives are -- of our war which were promptly defined and set before the Main Staff of the Army of the RS, the commands and units as a general guideline upon which we planned the actual operations and concerted battles." The evidence we presented show that the strategic objectives were immediately disseminated by the military. Two days later they were discussed at a meeting of municipality presidents. Five days later Subotic said that all conscripts had to be informed -- briefed of the goals. And five days later as well the commander for morale of the 1 KK said, specifically addressing strategic objective number 1: "The Serbian people must struggle for the complete separation from Muslim and Croat peoples to form their own state." Three weeks later directive 1 was issued by General Mladic and it called for operations to be conducted in order to realise the corridor. In fact, Your Honour, within six weeks of the directive -- of the strategic objectives being announced, the corridor operation was successful and the second strategic goal had been realised. The fourth directive that was issued in November of 1992 called for the removal of the Muslim population, and embedded throughout the army report are references, some of which mirror uncannily the exact words of the strategic objectives themselves. One reference in the army report says: "The strategic objective of our war would be realised, one that could be defined as 'establishing contact with Serbia on the river Drina, or the Drina ceasing to be a frontier.'" At the 34th Assembly Session Mladic described the relationship between military objectives and the political objectives of the war. He said: "Politics start and end the war." He went on to say that: "People and the army have carried out most of the tasks and the strategic goals set to them. We have created Republika Srpska." Finally I direct your attention to the testimony of General Wilson, who testified that military objectives and political objectives were indistinguishable. He said: "Operations of the Bosnian Serb army appeared to be directed at achieving the political aims that were quite clearly stated, that is setting up a separate Serb territory. It is no accident that the military operations seem to mirror requirements of the political ambitions." Lastly, Your Honour, let me turn my attention to an item that is addressed specifically in the Defence brief; the departure of the Muslims from Pale. In respect of this particular issue that seems to be in contention, Mr. Krajisnik testified that the Muslims left Pale municipality voluntarily, that he and Mr. Koljevic did not know of their departure from the Pale municipality until after they left. He learned of their departure sometime after 25 July 1992, and no one wanted the Muslims to leave. The Defence has invited the Chamber to pay the closest possible scrutiny to Defence Exhibits 197 through 216. We have done so and I'm going to direct Your Honours' attention to the contents of some of those documents. The first issue I'd like to address is: Was the departure of the Muslims from the Pale municipality voluntary? You heard the testimony of Sulejman Crncalo - he was a Muslim from Pale - and he described for Your Honours what life was like in Pale for the Muslims. He described intimidation of the Muslim community, random arrests, detentions, and beatings, calls for the Muslims to surrender their arms, Serb policemen coming to his community and telling Muslims it was better for them to leave. He described the meeting with Nikola Koljevic in May of 1992, who informed Mr. Crncalo and other members of his delegation of Muslims from Pale that "the Serbs don't want to go on living with you." He said Malko Koroman, the police chief from Pale, said that he couldn't protect the Muslim community of Pale, a statement that Mr. Crncalo took to be a threat. He went on to describe the restricted movement of Muslims because of check-points. They had to leave their property and leave with only the goods they could personally carry. He said Muslim telephone lines had been cut, paramilitaries had arrived and searched Muslim homes and intimidated the Muslim residents. Muslims were dismissed from working at the Famos factory. He described killings in the community. He described the arrival of 400 ethnically cleansed and beaten Muslims from the Bratunac area. And he concluded his testimony on this point by saying: "None of us wanted to leave our homes and our property and go out into the world like a beggar, but we had to." He said that he left the Pale municipality: "To save my life and the lives of my family members." The evidence of Omar -- Mr. Asim Omerovic, who was a 92 bis witness, described the attack on his village, described his own arrest, the fact that he was beaten and the beatings of others. So when you consider the testimonies of the witnesses you have heard on behalf of the Prosecution, consider, Your Honours, the events also that were occurring at the same time in other parts of Bosnia in municipalities that were occupied by the Bosnian Serbs. Now, if we examine the Defence documents, they support the testimony and the events described by Messrs. Crncalo and Omerovic. If Your Honours examine D197, minutes of a Pale Crisis Staff from the 9th of April, 1992, it shows that the delegation of Muslims went to the Crisis Staff and they presented proposals. Those proposals asked: "That events from other parts of SRBH not be reflected and reciprocally applied to the Muslim population in the territory of Pale municipality." He went on to say: "Families who do not feel safe be allowed to leave without hindrance due to reasons such as abuse, unlawful arrests of only Muslims, break-ins into apartments, disarming of Muslim police officers, seizing personal weapons with permits and similar." It's our submission, Your Honour, that the Muslims of the Pale municipality did not leave their homes in that community voluntarily. Now, Mr. Krajisnik testified that he had no knowledge that the Muslims from the Pale municipality had left. He only learned about that sometime after the 25th of July. Now, Pale's a small community; it's not New York City. It's not Tokyo. The 1991 census figures show that there were 16.355 people in the municipality, 7.384 lived in the town. We know for a fact that the town swelled with Serbian refugees. Mr. Divcic told us it swelled to 30.000. Nevertheless, it was a very small town. Mr. Krajisnik was clearly put on notice in May or June that Muslims and Croats wanted to leave his community. He testified that he had been visited by a Muslim and a Croat who informed him of that fact. On the 6th of July, 1992, if you examine Defence Exhibit 209, it reflects that a large percentage of the Muslims who had remained in Pale over a period of four days were placed on buses and escorted out of the municipality by Pale police officers. Specifically, it reflects that on the 30th of June, 88 Muslims left in two buses; on the 1st of July, 220 Muslims left on four buses; on the 2nd of July, 324 Muslims left on five buses; on the 3rd of July, 410 Muslims left on seven buses. That's a total of 1.042 Muslims out of this -- the small Muslim community that remained in the municipality. I'd also ask Your Honours to examine Defence Exhibit 208, a 6th July decision for an eight-bus convoy to escort 420 Muslims and Croats out of the municipality. That means in this small town of Pale, a significant percentage of the Muslim population left in organised convoys that surely Mr. Krajisnik must have been aware of and could not have failed to see. If the arrival of 400 Muslims from Bratunac was "the talk of the town" according to Mr. Divcic, the departure of a significant number of the remaining Muslims in that community must have been the talk of the town and must, Your Honours, have reached Mr. Krajisnik's ears. In addition, Your Honour, there was a -- on the 19th of June in Pale, there was a regulatory scheme set up to ensure the exchange of property. That regulatory scheme was similar in nature to what happened elsewhere in Bosnia. Mr. Krajisnik, in our submission, must have been aware of that, in his talks with Pale Crisis Staff representatives. Finally, Your Honours, if you look at Defence Exhibit 211, it's a document from the Pale municipality Crisis Committee dated the 7th of July that is addressed personally to Biljana Plavsic and informs Mrs. Plavsic that Muslims started moving out forcefully and wilfully at their own private initiate and discretion, and it goes on. Mrs. Plavsic surely would have shared that information with Mr. Krajisnik. Finally, Mr. Krajisnik asserts that no one waned the Pale Muslims to leave. I've already mentioned, Your Honour, a conversation that took place between Mr. Crncalo and Mr. Koljevic and the conversation that took place between Mr. Koroman, the police chief, and the large, organised convoys that escorted these people out. It is, of course, our submission, Your Honour, that the Muslim people who resided in Pale were forced out. It is also our submission, Your Honour, that their departure is consistent with the implementation of strategic objective number one, the strategic objective that Mr. Krajisnik said was the most important objective. Your Honour, I have concluded this part of the submissions. May I have just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to yield the floor to Mr. Gaynor, who will make the next set of submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'll be making submissions in response to ten legal issues which arise in the Defence final brief, and I'll then be making some short submissions on 7(3) responsibility. During the course of this, I'll be referring to several cases, and for later reference the citations to those cases are on a sheet which I've provided to Your Honours and to the Defence. The first of the ten issue issues is Rule 90(H)(ii). The Defence submits at paragraphs 62 to 69 of its brief that the Trial Chamber must not use important assertions as to acts and declarations of Mr. Krajisnik that were made by Prosecution witnesses and were not put to Mr. Krajisnik by the Prosecution in cross-examination. It relies on Rule 90(H)(ii), which provides: "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." The Defence submission does not cite to any jurisprudence in support of its position. Tribunal jurisprudence on Rule 90(H)(ii) and a national jurisprudence on a related principle known as the rule in Browne against Dunn, which was an English case cited in the early 1890s, do not support the Defence's assertion. Tribunal jurisprudence stresses that Rule 90(H) must be applied with a certain flexibility, depending on the general conduct of the trial. There is no absolute rule requiring a cross-examining party to put every detail of its version of the events to a witness or to put the witness on notice of every detail of the witness's evidence that the cross-examining party does not accept. In the application of the rule, a measure of flexibility will be allowed according to the circumstances, and based on the general conduct of the trial. Rule 90(H)(ii) is to be applied in a way to ensure the orderly progress of the trial and the transparent presentation of evidence. These principles appear in a Brdjanin and Talic decision of the 22nd of March, 2002, which examined the rationale behind Rule 90(H)(ii). That decision was upheld on appeal on 6 June 2002. The principles in those decisions were applied with approved by the Oric Trial Chamber in a decision of 17 January 2006. From the Tribunal's jurisprudence it is clear that Rule 90(H)(ii) is intended to secure three broad objectives: First, the rule protects against the possibility of a party ambushing a witness by not giving the witness an opportunity to state his position in respect of evidence which the cross-examining party later calls which contradicts the evidence of the witness. Second, the rule gives the Trial Chamber an opportunity to observe the witness's demeanour while he is confronted with contradictory evidence and while he comments on that evidence. Third - and this is a very practical consideration - the rule exists in order to avoid the need to bring a witness back to the Tribunal in order to deal with a new aspect of the cross-examining party's case which emerges from evidence later led by that party and which was not put to the witness when he or she first testified. Domestic jurisprudence accepts that this rule - it's the rule in Browne and Dunn - is not a strict rule at all and was not intended to be by the court in Browne and Dunn itself but is rather a principle that applies to a greater or lesser extent depending on the particular facts of the case and the conduct of the trial. In particular, ambush of a witness is avoided where the witness is put on objectively sufficient notice that his credibility is in issue. Where the witness is the accused, there is jurisprudence to the effect that the Rule does not apply. I will very briefly draw Your Honours' attention to four domestic decisions on the rule in Browne and Dunn. First in Verney, a case concerning the application of the rule to the Defence, the Ontario Court of Appeal said that the rule: "Is not an absolute rule and counsel must not feel obliged to slog through a witness's evidence in chief, putting him on notice of every detail the Defence does not accept." The Court added that: "Counsel must be free to use his own judgement about how to cross-examine a hostile witness. Having the witness repeat in cross-examination everything he said in chief is rarely the tactic of choice." Second, in a 1983 Australian decision, Allied Pastoral Holdings against the Federal Commissioner of Taxation, recently cited with approval by the English Court of Appeal case in Markem Corporation against Zipher Limited, Judge David Hunt - the same Judge David Hunt who later acted here - noted that Browne against Dunn itself recognised that there was no obligation to raise a matter in cross-examination in circumstances where it was perfectly clear that the witness had full notice beforehand that there was an intention to impeach the credibility of the story which he was telling. Another Australian case, Raben Footwear against Polygram, said that the rule in Browne and Dunn: "may be satisfied where the witness is on notice that the version given is disputed, and such notice may come from pleadings, the opponent's evidence or opening, or from the general manner in which the case is conducted." The fourth and final case is the Crown against W. (M. L.). There the Ontario Court of Appeal found that when the witness was the accused, this was not a Browne and Dunn situation. The Court said: "There was no ambush of the appellant. He knew the case against him full well when he went into the witness box. There was no evidence called by the Crown in reply. It is a matter of judgement on the part of Crown counsel as to what areas he wishes to cross-examine on." Similarly, in this case, there was no ambush of any kind. The accused was well aware of the Prosecution's case against him when he began his testimony, and he was given an opportunity to answer that case, and he took that opportunity over the course of 40 days of testimony. Before the accused began to give evidence, he had received the indictment, the supporting material, a great deal of pre-trial disclosure, and the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. He had heard the Prosecution's opening statement, the oral evidence of 93 Prosecution witnesses, he had received written evidence of many more, and also received over 3.800 Prosecution exhibits during the course of the trial. He had also listened to the Prosecution's cross-examination of 24 Defence witnesses. In addition, he met with his counsel frequently throughout the trial and, in particular, prior to the beginning of his testimony. The accused was therefore on full notice of the Prosecution's case against him. In fact, almost his entire evidence in chief was a response to that case. Therefore, there can be no concern about the accused being put on notice as to the essence of the Prosecution's case against him and being given the opportunity to respond to that case. It is also relevant that there was no rebuttal case for the Prosecution. So there was no practical issue about re-calling the accused to respond to further Prosecution evidence. In respect of assessing credibility, the Chamber had ample opportunity to observe the accused and to draw its own conclusions about the accused's credibility during the 40 days of his evidence. For these reasons, all the concerns underlying Rule 90(H)(ii) were addressed. Prosecution complied with Rule 90(H)(ii) in accordance with the spirit and the aim of the rule and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. We submit that there is, therefore, no merit in the Defence submissions concerning Rule 90(H)(ii). The second point, the mens rea for planning, ordering, and instigating in the Defence brief is incorrect. The submissions set out at paragraphs 92 to 96 of the Defence brief in relation to those three forms of liability do not refer to and are not consistent with the definitions of the actus reus and the mens rea for planning, ordering, and instigating set out at paragraphs 25 to 32 of the Kordic appeal judgement. The threshold set out at those paragraphs is lower than the test set out in the Defence brief. The next point is that joint criminal enterprise liability can apply to a massive criminal campaign. The Defence appears to argue, at paragraphs 107 and 130 to 134 of its brief, that JCE liability cannot apply in a large-scale case. This issue has already been considered and dismissed -- this argument has been dismissed by the ICTR Appeals Chamber. In the Karemera decision of 12th April 2006, the Appeals Chamber found that there is no geographical limitation on JCE liability. Liability can apply to a JCE of vast scope. Further support is found in paragraph 25 of the Rwamakuba decision of the ICTR Appeals Chamber of the 22nd October, 2004, where the Appeals Chamber noted that post-World War II jurisprudence, in particular the Justice case, shows that liability for participation in a criminal plan is as wide as the plan itself, even if the plan amounts to a nation-wide government-organised system of cruelty and injustice. Fourth point: The application of JCE 3, liability to genocide, was recognised under customary international law in 1992 and was sufficiently accessible to the accused at the time of the offences. The Defence, at paragraphs 245 to 253 and 259 of its brief, argues that the application of JCE 3 to genocide would offend the nullum crimen principle. In particular, the Defence argues that the Rwamakuba decision of 22nd October 2004 did not expressly address the question of whether JCE liability was recognised in customary law prior to 1992. Now, the Appeals Chamber in Rwamakuba found that the customary international law recognised the application of JCE liability to the crime of genocide before 1992. The Chamber did not exclude JCE 3 from its finding. Further, the Chamber expressly declared correct a statement to the effect that JCE liability applied to genocide in the Tadic appeal judgement, which concerns all three forms of JCE liability. In addition, the Rwamakuba decision refers several times to the ICTY Appeals Chamber's 19 March 2004 decision in Brdjanin that JCE 3 and genocide are compatible. Therefore, our submission is that the Karemera decision of the 12th of April, 2006, when read in conjunction with the Rwamakuba decision, confirm that the application of JCE 3 to genocide was recognised in customary law in 1992. I refer Your Honours expressly to footnote 41 of the decision of the 12th of April, 2006. Now, the Defence argues at paragraph 256 of its brief that JCE 3 for genocide was not sufficiently foreseeable to the accused in 1992. The Appeals Chamber, in its 21st of May, 2003, decision in Milutinovic ruled that JCE liability - and it did not exclude JCE 3 liability - was sufficiently foreseeable. Its decision was in the context of a Kosovo case, but it relied in part on the -- on Article 26 of the 1977 Criminal Code of the SFRY. The next point is that JCE does not require an agreement between the accused and those physically carrying out the crimes. The Defence brief, at paragraphs 148 to 150, argues that for JCE liability to attach, the Chamber must be satisfied that the Prosecution has proved that there was an understanding or agreement to commit a particular crime between the accused and the relevant physical perpetrators. The Defence argues that the fact that both may have espoused a strategic plan is not equivalent to an arrangement between them to commit a concrete crime, and they rely on the Brdjanin judgement. We submit that the requirement referred to by the Defence does not exist and the Brdjanin judgement is erroneous in this regard. Two different issues have to be distinguished: First, does the physical perpetrator need to be a member of the JCE? Second, do the members of the JCE have to have an agreement, and what is its content? In respect of the first issue, we submit that it is not necessary that the physical perpetrators be JCE members. It is possible to have a JCE made up of members at the leadership level who use the physical perpetrators as their instruments or tools. The Prosecution's position, which is set out in Prosecution's appeal brief in Brdjanin, that the physical perpetrators do not need to be among the members of the JCE has been implicitly confirmed in paragraphs 63 to 98 of the Stakic appeal judgement and is supported by Judge Bonomy's separate opinion in Milutinovic of the 22nd of March, 2006. With regard to the second issue, the question whether, if the physical perpetrators are among the members of the JCE there needs to be a direct agreement between the physical perpetrators and the accused, is also currently under appeal in Brdjanin. The only support cited in the Brdjanin judgement for the existence of this requirement is an interlocutory decision in Brdjanin of the 26th of June, 2001, which itself cites no authority. Neither Tribunal jurisprudence nor customary international law support this narrow interpretation of JCE liability. The Prosecution's position on appeal in Brdjanin is that it is sufficient if the members of the JCE espouse the same plan, design, or purpose. As I mentioned earlier, it has been recognised by the ICTR Appeals Chamber that a JCE can be nation-wide. If this is the case, it clearly cannot be a requirement for responsibility of the members of the JCE that they all have entered into something akin to a one-to-one understanding or agreement with each other. The application of JCE liability by the Appeals Chamber in Stakic and by Trial Chamber -- the Trial Chamber in Krstic, and by the Chambers in plea agreement cases such as Obrenovic and Plavsic, shows that a direct agreement between the accused and the physical perpetrators is not required. Significantly, a number of post-Brdjanin Appeals Chamber interlocutory decisions and judgements concerning JCE have not referred to such a requirement. Therefore, in the present case, in accordance with the approach taken in the Stakic appeal judgement, this Trial Chamber is not required to find that the physical perpetrators were members of the JCE. And if it does find that the physical perpetrators were members of the JCE, it does not have to find that there was an understanding or agreement to commit a particular crime between the accused and the relevant physical perpetrators in addition to proof of the existence of the common plan, design, or purpose espoused by the members of the JCE. Sixth point - and it's a short one - JCE liability does not require that the accused make a substantial contribution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, before you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to the position of the Prosecution which was set out in the Brdjanin appeals brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that required a lot of paragraphs I think you referred to. Is that the position the OTP takes in general or just in Brdjanin or would it fully apply here? How do we have to understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, you can understand that as being the Prosecution position in this case also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's our policy -- position. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Legal analysis, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. The analysis we've made in the Brdjanin is also applied by the Prosecution in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's -- that's clear, then. That's on the judicial database, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can provide you with the date. Your Honours, the Prosecution's brief on appeal in the Brdjanin case is the 28th of January, 2005, and I refer Your Honours in particular to pages 5 to 20 of that brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the sixth point is that JCE liability does not require that the accused make a substantial contribution. The Defence brief states at paragraph 143 that for JCE liability to attach, "the accused must have carried out acts that substantially assisted or significantly effected the furtherance of the goals of the enterprise." The brief cites to the Kvocka trial judgement but fails to refer to the Kvocka appeal judgement, which held at paragraph 97 that there is no specific legal requirement that the accused make a substantial contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. The next point - also short - the Defence brief, at paragraphs 152 to 154, makes submissions concerning aiding and abetting a joint criminal enterprise. I direct Your Honours to the Kvocka appeal judgement at paragraph 91 where the Appeals Chamber held that it is inaccurate to refer to aiding and abetting a joint criminal enterprise, but rather the aider and abettor assists the principal perpetrator or perpetrators in committing the crime. The eighth point is that superior responsibility for genocide does not require proof of special intent. The Defence final brief, at paragraphs 260, 266 to 270, submits that for a conviction for genocide under Article 7(3), the Prosecution must establish that the accused possessed the requisite dolus specialis. The only support for this view is the Stakic Rule 98 bis decision. As the Defence brief appears to accept, there is a considerable quantity of jurisprudence against the Defence on this point. In the Brdjanin decision on interlocutory appeal on the 19th of March, 2004, the Appeals Chamber referred to command responsibility liability as an example of a form of liability which does not require proof of intent to commit a crime on the part of the accused in order for a criminal liability to attach. I refer Your Honours to the Brdjanin trial judgement, paragraphs 717 to 721, the Blagojevic trial judgement, paragraphs 686, the Milosevic 98 bis decision at paragraph 300. All of those Trial Chambers took the view that specific intent on the part of the accused is not necessary for finding of genocide under Article 7(3).

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next point concerns the expanded Presidency. Mr. Tieger has made submissions about the expanded or War Presidency already. To his submissions, and I refer to the Defence brief at paragraph 198, I simply wish to add that as a matter of law it is not in fact necessary to prove that the accused held any de jure authority to secure a conviction under Article 7(3). A finding of de jure authority does establish a rebuttable presumption of effective control, but the controlling test for liability to attach is whether the accused in fact held effective control in the sense of a material ability to prevent or punish conduct however that control is exercised and regardless of the formality of his appointment or the titles which he held. And I refer the Court to the discussion in the Celebici appeal judgement paragraph 197. The tenth legal point is the accused's intent to commit crimes in each indictment municipality. The Defence submits that the Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Krajisnik intended the commission of crimes in each of the indictment municipalities and suggests that this analysis must take place with respect to each and every specific offence or event charged and it is not sufficient to infer it from the existence of some general or overarching purpose. That's at paragraph 138 of their brief. The Defence cites no authority for this proposition. The Kvocka appeals judgement at paragraph 276 demonstrates that a participant in the JCE does not need to know of each crime committed in order to be criminally liable, where a series of charged acts forms part of an attack of a discriminatory nature, this context can be a sufficient basis to infer the discriminatory intent in relation to each particular act. In respect of that proposition the support is the Blagojevic trial judgement at paragraph 584 and the Tadic trial judgement at paragraph 652. Rather than carrying out a site-by-site compartmentalised analysis, we submit that the Chamber must consider the evidence in this case as a whole in determining whether the accused intended to commit the crimes in each indictment municipality. That means considering as a whole the evidence concerning, for example, disarming the non-Serb population, arming and training the Serb population, establishing Crisis Staffs, establishing Serb-only police and TO forces, dismissal of non-Serbs from employment, coordinated take-overs of power at the municipal level by Crisis Staffs and Serb forces, shelling and burning houses and other civilian targets, detention, mass killings, and expulsions of great numbers of Muslims and Croats, including through the provision of organised transportation out of the indictment municipalities --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- and the systematic elimination of Muslim and Croat sacred sites. The Chamber must consider that evidence in conjunction with the related evidence of neutral international observers; MUP, VRS, Crisis Staff documentation; victim and insider evidence; statements of the Bosnian Serb leadership; as well as evidence identifying the territories targeted for inclusion in the Serb state as evidence from which to infer a centrally directed, massive and systematic attack on the Muslim and Croat populations in all of the indictment municipalities. In the Stakic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber, quite rightly, noted that where the accused is hierarchically distant from the physical perpetrators: "To require proof of the discriminatory intent of both the accused and the acting individuals in relation to all the single acts committed would lead to an unjustifiable protection of superiors and would run counter to the meaning, spirit, and purpose of the Statute of this International Tribunal." Your Honours, that ends the purely legal submissions for the moment. I will now make submissions on 7(3) liability of this accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that means factual submissions or -- because you said that ends the legal submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. These are not -- I know Your Honours have given us some legal questions on 7(3), which I propose to address at a later date. These are just a quick overview of our factual position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we first start with the facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Krajisnik and Karadzic were at the apex of the Bosnian Serb structure of power. Together with others, they designed, developed, and promoted the common purpose and oversaw and directed the establishment of bodies and organs to secure its implementation. They intended that crimes be committed during the brutal campaign to secure the objective of pure territories. As the architects and implementers of that campaign, they had no incentive to devote resources to preventing crimes committed in pursuit of that campaign, nor to punish the perpetrators of those crimes. Our position is that the Bosnian Serb leadership, with Karadzic and Krajisnik at its apex, had the material ability to prevent and punish the commission of crimes by the VRS, including paramilitary forces incorporated in the VRS, from its creation on the 12th of May, 1992, until at least 30th December, 1992; and over the Serb TO, the RS MUP, including paramilitary forces incorporated in the TO and the MUP, and Serb Crisis Staffs from the 1st of April, 1992, until at least the 30th of December, 1992. Instead of preventing or punishing, the Bosnian Serb authorities deliberately created a culture of impunity for brutal crimes against non-Serbs, while continuing to arrest and prosecute Serbs committing ordinary crimes, including relatively minor crimes against fellow Serbs. The Serb Republic continued to insist on a facade of legality and forced thousands of non-Serbs fleeing the claimed territory to sign documents purporting to lawfully transfer title to their property to the Serb Republic. But when it came to enforcing the law in respect of brutal crimes against Muslims and Croats, the Serb authorities did next to nothing. In respect of the MUP, the existence of a culture of impunity and the deliberate non-prosecution of MUP members for crimes against non-Serbs, including mass killings conducted in circumstances of shocking brutality, is evident from the lack of any real effort to prosecute those responsible for crimes such as the brutal Koricanje Stijene massacre discussed at the Presidency session at which the accused was present on the 1st of September, 1992, and the other crimes referred to at paragraph 317 of our brief. In respect of the VRS, the existence of a culture of impunity for crimes against non-Serbs was evident from a great body of evidence, including the evidence referred to at paragraphs 406 and 407 of our brief. The VRS took steps to prevent individual looting by Serb soldiers for their personal profit, but took no meaningful action to punish soldiers who participated in mass killings of Croats and Muslims. As the Banja Luka military court log and the Banja Luka military prosecutor's log, which are in evidence, illustrate, prosecutions initiated against soldiers for crimes against non-Serbs were allowed to lapse. Those few soldiers who were taken into custody for brutal massacres were quietly released back into their units. Soldiers felt immune, and indeed were immune, from prosecutions for crimes committed against non-Serbs. The same applied to paramilitaries. As we said at paragraph 336 of the brief, Yellow Wasps were arrested in Zvornik. They were arrested for stealing cars, but the authorities were aware that those Yellow Wasps were involved killings of Muslims in Celopek. None of the Yellow Wasps were prosecuted for killing Muslims, but instead, several were offered positions in the RS MUP intelligence services. Even when the brutality of conditions within several Serb detention facilities became front-page news around the world in August 1992, the leadership took no effective action against the perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, we usually say to witnesses: Wait until the text stops moving. I'm not asking you to always keep an eye on the screen, but your speed of speech is still a bit high.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On the 6th of August, the Presidency issued a decision that a commission for investigation of war crimes against Serbs should start its work. The minutes of the meeting also record that the Presidency directed the MUP to investigate; however, both the MUP inquiry and government commissions of inquiry which were also set up were a mere sham, as we submit in paragraphs 454 to 456 of our brief. The Trial Chamber, on several occasions, invited Defence witnesses to submit evidence of proper investigations and prosecutions of crimes against Serbs. No meaningful evidence was submitted, to our knowledge. It is also relevant that during the entire Defence case, the Defence did not submit any convincing evidence of any meaningful effort to prosecute. The burden of proof remains on the Prosecution to prove liability under Article 7(3), but in our submission the Court may, in assessing whether that burden has been met, also take into account in the exercise of its discretion the nature of its responses to its invitations for evidence of meaningful prosecution. There can be no doubt that the Presidency, including Mr. Krajisnik, had the power to take steps to protect Muslim and Croat populations. To name just one area, it had the power to order the release of the thousands of Muslims and Croats detained in conditions of great brutality. Following the international outrage which resulted from news of conditions in many of the camps, the Presidency, on the 6th of September, did exercise its power to release and ordered the release of a token number of prisoners from Manjaca. As well as failing to take action to protect Muslims and Croats, when implored to do so by neutral international humanitarian organisations, the accused took steps to keep the issue of prisoners off the agenda at the Serb Assembly. At the 10th of August, 1992, Assembly session, the accused deftly and effectively removed the prisoners issue from the Assembly's agenda. He was also fully involved in the Bosnian Serb leadership's decision, illustrated by the 8th August Presidency minutes, to solve the prisoner issue by insisting in international negotiations on a system of all-for-all exchanges. In short, the accused took next to no action to prevent the commission of crimes or to hold to account those responsible. In his testimony he took the position that if he had known about the crimes, he would have intervened or asked for a debate or demanded that those responsible take steps or speak out within the Presidency, but he also took the position that he would have been powerless even if he did speak out. The accused's position that even if he did disapprove of crimes, he could do nothing, is simply not credible. He was a member of the inner core of the Bosnian Serb leadership, which had effective control over MUP, VRS, TO, paramilitary forces operating under the direction of those bodies, and Crisis Staffs. Rather than seeking to prevent or punish crimes, the accused actively participated in the preparation for and the implementation of the campaign for ethnic separation. He continued to work hard as that campaign grew to tragic proportions with such devastating consequences for thousands of Muslims and Croats. Now, I'll hand back to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. To both of them; are they speaking simultaneously? Mr. Tieger or Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to address the issue of credibility generally and specifically in this case. Your Honours have heard the testimonies of 124 witnesses and have reviewed the testimonies of 97 statements admitted under 92 bis without cross-examination. You and the Judges must determine the truthfulness and the accuracy of each witness's statement and each witness's testimony, and in that regard, Your Honours, in making those separate assessments as to whether a witness who took the oath of solemn declaration before this Court told the truth or did not tell the truth, we, as experienced advocates and you as experienced Judges, know that there's no particular formula to apply in evaluating whether a witness has told the truth. Instead, you must apply your varied experiences in life in making judgements as to whether a witness told the truth or didn't tell the truth. If, however, Your Honours find that any witness has intentionally lied after taking the oath and lied about a material fact, you can disregard that witness's testimony in its entirety, or you can accept as much of it as you find may have been truthfully given. Now, in its brief the Defence has directed your attention to various categories of witnesses called by the Prosecution and has made certain observations about those categories. I'd like to respond to that, and I will do so now. The first category that the Defence identified is witnesses called by the Prosecution, they were convicts, and he identified them by name, omitting, of course, that the Trial Chamber also called a convict, Biljana Plavsic. The Defence made a very serious and provocative allegation when it asserted that the Prosecution does not call witnesses as some sort of fact-finding exercise or search for the truth. And I state now publicly that we categorically and emphatically reject that assertion. We also categorically reject the assertion in the Defence brief that no Prosecutor could call criminals such as these individuals unless they felt that they simply had no other option and in relying on their evidence, the Office of the Prosecutor were really scraping the barrel. While these characterisations are unnecessary and untrue, I want to deal with reality. Mr. Krajisnik was part of a criminal enterprise. The persons who were close to him and who were also engaged in the enterprise and were convicted of crimes related to the enterprise are ideally the persons who are likely to know information and have evidence that's vital to the search for the truth. It's also important to bear in mind that the "convicts" called by the Office of the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber did not testify about events in isolation. Considerable testimonial evidence corroborated the particulars of their testimony. In addition, witnesses who testified before this Court corroborated their evidence. In assessing whether a witness's criminal conviction has affected the truthfulness of the witness's testimony, I'm quite confident that you will measure his or her testimony in light of all the evidence that's been presented during this case and will find their evidence to be reliable. Second, the Defence brief draws attention to the category of suspects. I want to be clear from the outset. With the exception of Mr. Mandic, who is facing criminal proceedings in Bosnia, none of the persons identified as suspects by the Defence, to my knowledge, has been declared so by the Bosnian authorities. The Defence invites you to engage in speculation. The reality is that many of these "suspects" are persons who were close to Mr. Krajisnik personally and/or professionally during the period of the indictment. As such, they are persons who had considerable insight into Mr. Krajisnik's conduct and into the organs of government of which he and they were members. Again, Your Honours, examine carefully who they were and examine if these persons were persons who had an opportunity to see or to hear the events about which they testified, if their evidence is plausible and likely to be true in light of the other evidence you received, and whether they had any hostility or bias towards Mr. Krajisnik. The expert category highlighted the testimony of Messrs. Treanor, Nielsen, Ms. Hanson and Mr. Browne. It's undisputed that three of them are employed by the Office of the Prosecutor, and Mr. Brown was employed by the Office of the Prosecutor at the time he prepared his report. You're urged by the Defence to examine that element and conclude or at least examine their conclusions with caution because it's asserted they are not independent. Those experts who testified and who presented reports to Your Honours, we don't ask you to rely on their bald assertions in those reports. Those reports were supported by documentation that was voluminous in some cases. We invite you to scrutinise their evidence, their conclusions, the materials upon which they base their conclusions when you make a judgement as to their reliability. Again, also compare their conclusions and their findings with the other evidence that you've heard in this case, both Defence witnesses, Prosecution witnesses, and Trial Chamber witnesses. When we turn to the fourth category, internationals, you're urged to scrutinise international witnesses who testified here. The international witnesses who testified here were Mr. Charles Kirudja, General John Wilson, former Ambassador Okun, two witnesses from international organisations who testified with protective measures and one who gave written evidence pursuant to 94 bis. You're urged to treat their evidence with care. According to the Defence brief, many of the international witnesses "had developed a built-in antipathy toward Serbs and developed a rather biased disposition and were not objectively reliable." We reject those assertions. The international witnesses who came and gave evidence before you were not parties to this conflict, but were persons who represented neutral international organisations and who had unique access to Bosnian Serb military and political leaders, including Mr. Krajisnik, and were fully aware of the situation in the field in Bosnia. In some cases, their contemporaneous reports are before you. In many instances those reports reflect the critical view of the crimes that were taking place and the events that they observed while they were in the field, but having a critical view doesn't make them objectively unreliable as witnesses. Again, Your Honours, apply your common sense and the standards that you normally would apply as Judges to the testimonies of these neutral third parties, whose evidence you heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Finally, let me turn to a witness whose evidence was specifically identified, Mr. Davidovic. The Defence states in its brief that it was noteworthy that Mr. Davidovic became a witness "relatively late in the case," and was called because "the Prosecution felt that their case was lacking." The Defence claimed in trial and claims again in its brief that Mr. Davidovic is a liar, that he knew and sanctioned torture, and that the Prosecution in calling him were scraping the barrel. Let me first address what the Defence fails to mention in its brief as to the reason why Mr. Davidovic became a witness late in the proceedings. These facts were contained in the Prosecution's motion of 8 April 2005 and were summarised in the Trial Chamber's decision on that motion at page 12.461 of the transcript. Mr. Davidovic declined to be interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in the absence of a waiver from his government. Despite repeated requests and reminders by the Office of the Prosecutor, the FRY government delayed for nearly two years issuing a required waiver. And when they were finally issued in October of 2004, the Prosecutor interviewed Mr. Davidovic. Those interviews concluded in March of 2005. We then added Mr. Davidovic to our witness list in early April of 2005. The Defence attacks on Mr. Davidovic have been relentless. In the brief they called him a liar. In trial proceedings they called him a liar. The Defence in no way were curtailed from bringing evidence aimed at influencing the Trial Chamber's perception of his credibility. They brought no evidence before this Chamber. At trial they called him a criminal, asserting there were criminal proceedings pending against him. They accused him from taking property from Muslims during the war, attacks that were not true and later withdrawn by the Defence. I want to address those issues further. Those issues have already been addressed by the Chamber. Finally, the Defence invites the Trial Chamber to find that Davidovic must have "known and sanctioned the torture that his men doled out on their captives." This invitation is based in part on the testimony of KRAJ 682, which the Trial Chamber noted was based on "speculation conclusions rather than clear observation of facts." I direct Your Honours' attention to 17.016 and 017. I further note, Your Honour, that the Defence produced no evidence revealing a demonstrated animus of Mr. Davidovic toward Mr. Krajisnik. At trial they asserted that because he didn't have a single word of praise for Mr. Krajisnik he was biased, nothing more. That's found at 14.358. Likewise, they suggested that he lied about Krajisnik to cover up his own misconduct. That's found at 15.229. That criminal conduct, allegations of which, were later withdrawn. What's important, however, having said that, is that Mr. Davidovic's evidence should be analysed like any other witness in this case. You should apply the same standards. Despite the vociferous attacks on him, we invite you to apply those standards to Mr. Davidovic's testimony like you would any other witness. Now, Your Honours, having addressed those points, I would like to turn to the credibility of Mr. Krajisnik, and I've addressed Mr. Krajisnik's credibility in part in my previous submissions. I'll cite some but not all of the points where it is our belief Mr. Krajisnik was not truthful. In assessing his credibility, I'd urge you to examine particular -- the plain meaning of his words that he uttered in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, in Assembly sessions, in interviews, in speeches, and compare them with the contorted meanings he attached to his words during the course of his evidence. Consider also whether, in light of other evidence you've heard in the course of this trial, his evidence is plausible or likely to be true. Let's start with the issue of Mr. Krajisnik's testimony relating to his lack of knowledge about Bosnian Serbs being armed before the conflict. We spent considerable time on that topic. Mr. Krajisnik testified: "I do not know in which way and how they were arming themselves." In response to a question by Judge Hanoteau, Mr. Krajisnik answered: "But I emphasise that I did not have any information at the time that the Serb side was arming itself." He's testified again later: "As for the things I heard second-hand, stories circulated that people were receiving weapons, and I heard some stories like that, like rumours, but nothing specific." He said that arming was a secret. Perhaps people spoke about it only tete-a-tete. He wants you to believe, Your Honours, that he was ignorant about the fact that the Serbs were being armed prior to the conflict. Here was a leader who was specifically concerned that his people were at risk of genocide, that they found themselves in a minority in an Independent State of Bosnia and he knew nothing about any means by which they would protect themselves if necessary. He testified that he and Karadzic met with the top echelons of the JNA in Sarajevo and in Belgrade before the war. Given the fact that the Bosnian Serb leadership's concerns about possible genocide against the Serb people, is it logical that he was unaware that the JNA, parties with whom he'd met in Belgrade and Sarajevo, were not supplying arms to the Bosnian Serbs? We submit it is not. Our evidence shows that he was fully aware of the arming programme that was taking place. Both General Gvero at the 34th Session and other members of the Assembly testified or stated in those meetings that the Serbian Democratic Party, and I quote General Gvero: "The Serbian Democratic Party and the established state institutions also have the most credit for the initial arming of the Serb people ..." P51, a report -- a top-secret report prepared by General Kukanjac, referred to many, many times in the course of this trial, indicates that: "The JNA distributed 51.900 pieces of armament and the SDS 17.298 pieces." That same report mentions that General Kukanjac would be meeting with Bosnian Serb leaders, who he identified, including Mr. Krajisnik. Now, it's our submission that the arming of the Serbs was widespread and notorious. If you look at Sarajevo municipality alone, a subject of keen interest of Mr. Krajisnik, and you look at the Kukanjac report, you can see that 15.100 weapons were distributed in the Sarajevo municipalities, and in Mr. Krajisnik's municipality 2.400 weapons were distributed. The persons who were engaged in the arming efforts, you've heard evidence who some of them were: Radovan Karadzic, Goran Zekic, Danilo Veselinovic, SDS Main Board member Jovan Tintor, Mr. Krajisnik's kum, Rajko Djukic, president of the SDS Executive Board, General Kukanjac, who was the commander of the 2nd Military District. Mr. Krajisnik -- let's focus on one person who should have caught the attention of Mr. Krajisnik, that's Dusan Kosic, who was a prominent member of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, who was arrested for smuggling arms on the 24th of May, 1991. He smuggled ten crates -- or eight crates of automatic weapons. Lots of ammunition. This was a notorious event. It made the headlines in Oslobodjenje. Mr. Karadzic publicly spoke about it at a press conference. Mr. Krajisnik's evidence on that? A member of parliament who had asked for immunity, he said he didn't know anything about it. Simply not credible, Your Honour. Furthermore, there are intercepts, two intercepts, that deal with Mr. Krajisnik being directly informed of weapons. Mr. Djukic talked to him about buying 1.000 weapons, Mr. Karadzic talked to him about the Serbs not having enough weapons. So it's our submission, Your Honour, that Mr. Krajisnik was not truthful when he said he did not know about the Serbs being armed. Let's focus briefly on the shelling of Sarajevo. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we need another break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether this would be an appropriate moment before --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are aware that we have a break of 20 minutes, that means that we'll resume at 6.20 sharp, and the Prosecution has another 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the beginning of our presentation we lost, I think, 15 minutes by virtue of -- I'll have to check, but there was a decision that was read that -- we'd finely tuned our timing on this. I was wondering whether or not those minutes would be returned to the Prosecution or not during the break; we can otherwise adjust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but not -- I'll see how much time I took for reading. That's always a dilemma because if I read too quickly, I'm making the same mistake as many do in this court-room; if I read too slowly, then the interpreters are suffering in a different way, and that is that you ask for more time after 7.00. I'll consider the matter. I also noted, Mr. Harmon, that when points were discussed where the briefs clearly indicate that the parties take a different view, that sometimes also reference was made to matters I remember having read clearly already in the brief. A shorter reference would certainly have served. So if you would keep that in mind and discuss with your colleagues how you'll manage to finish by 7.00. Then I'll have a look at how much time it took me to read. We'll adjourn until 20 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please proceed. It took me eight minutes and five seconds to read the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in respect of those eight minutes and five seconds, Your Honour, is there any decision reached on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's see. I think if you don't speak too quickly and if you behave well, I certainly would think that the interpreters would assist you in five minutes or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'll begin. The next issue I'd like to address is on the issue of Mr. Krajisnik's credibility, deals with the shelling of Sarajevo. In that context Mr. Krajisnik testified: "Let me repeat, and I think this is important: Whether somebody shelled or will shell Sarajevo or not was something the army decided." He also said he did not "remember that there was any major shelling of Sarajevo ever." Your Honours, recall the testimony of General John Wilson who was the head of the UNMOs for UNPROFOR in Sarajevo. He described a massive shelling on the 14th of May, 1992. In his own words, he said Sarajevo suffered a horrific artillery bombardment. On the order of 5 to 10.000 rounds of artillery were fired on the city that day. He said it was indiscriminate, disproportionate. He'd never seen such a weight of fire used, particularly against civilian targets. It seemed to him there was no value, military value in the targets selected. As a result of that, Your Honour, UNPROFOR moved its headquarters, moved to Belgrade. That a major shelling incident resulted in the displacement of one of the most significant international organisations operating in Bosnia is surely something that did not escape the attention of Mr. Krajisnik. I direct Your Honours' attention also to the minutes of the fourth expanded meeting of the War Presidency of 9 June, 1992, with Mr. Krajisnik in attendance at that Presidency session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I was under the impression that we would start in private session. I had not ordered that. I do not see that confirmed on my screen; therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can speak publicly on these matters, Your Honour. I'm going to go into private session in just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was directing Your Honours' attention to the minutes of the fourth expanded meeting of the War Presidency on the 9th of June, with Mr. Krajisnik in attendance, and after having been briefed by General Mladic and his other generals who were present, there was a conclusion reached at that session: "The heavy artillery fire on the town be halted." And if you look at another event, also ultimately reflected in the Presidency session minutes, the minutes relate that after the Presidency had received or became aware of the Secretary-General statement that had been issued to the Security Council, complaining about the artillery attack on areas -- heavy artillery attack on areas of Dobrinja that threatened the airport negotiations, the following day at the 12th Session of the Presidency, which Mr. Krajisnik attended and Mr. Karadzic did not, they reflect that: "The Main Staff is ordered to cease all artillery and infantry operations in the suburb of Dobrinja immediately." This is undisputed evidence that Mr. Krajisnik's testimony that the shelling of Sarajevo was something that the army decided was not the case. The shelling of Sarajevo was a political decision implemented by the military that could be turned on and off depending on the circumstances. Now if we could go into private session for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on the evidence that I have reviewed and other evidence that's been presented to this Court, it is our submission, Your Honour, that the shelling of Sarajevo wasn't decided exclusively by the military. Mr. Krajisnik was fully aware of massive shellings that were taking place on Sarajevo. A last issue I want to address briefly is the issue of the separation of the police, because this is another issue where Mr. Krajisnik squarely puts his credibility at issue. The -- on the 31st of March Mr. Mandic sent a dispatch that resulted in the separation of the police. It created a crisis. Mr. Krajisnik's evidence on that was that he was in Brussels at the time and he and Karadzic were stunned to receive news that this dispatch had been sent out. And according to Mr. Krajisnik, he said it was unauthorised, it was an irresponsible act that took them by surprise, they were stunned, and that he -- he had no time to do anything to rectify or negate and manage this irresponsible and unauthorised act. He wanted to distance himself from what Mr. Mandic did. Recall that Mr. Mandic -- Mr. Krajisnik took a very legalistic approach as to whether or not that dispatch was legally authorised. He avoided the core issue. The core issue was that he and Mr. Karadzic agreed with what Mr. Mandic had done. This is demonstrated in fact by the failure - his failure, Mr. Karadzic's failure - to immediately repudiate the act of Mr. Mandic or to take any ameliorative steps such as simply sending a dispatch to all the police stations affected and saying: Disregard it. How simple is that? Mr. Krajisnik's assertion that there was not enough time is simply beggar's belief. How long would it have taken for him to issue a memorandum, forward it through the normal channels? An hour? Six hours? A day? Nothing happened. But Mico Stanisic, the minister of the interior, found time three days later to send a dispatch to the police station saying Mandic's dispatch was operative. Now, finally, what also supports the fact that Mr. Krajisnik was not truthful are his actions that he took vis-a-vis Mr. Zepinic, who was the highest ranking police official in the Bosnian government. Remember, Mr. Zepinic -- Dr. Zepinic was meeting with members -- with Delimustafic, his superior and members of the special police unit in an attempt to keep them an integrated unit when he was summoned to the office of Mr. Krajisnik, summoned by Mr. Krajisnik personally. When Dr. Zepinic arrived in the office of Mr. Krajisnik, present were Mr. Mandic, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Djeric, Mr. Buha, and others, and he was vigorously attacked because he had been meeting with the special police unit and not supporting the division of the special police. According to Mr. Mandic, the division of the special police was the final act in the division of the MUP. Dr. Zepinic offered to submit his resignation to Mr. Krajisnik; that was accepted. It doesn't sound like the actions of someone who didn't have time to do anything; it sounds, in our submission, like the actions of someone who firmly supported Mr. Mandic's efforts to divide the police. And it's our submission that Mr. Krajisnik did have time to take affirmative steps to repudiate the dispatch. Mr. Krajisnik supported the division of the police at the time Mr. Mandic sent the dispatch, and his testimony about not having time to do so was false and was an attempt to mislead this Trial Chamber on this issue. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I yield the floor to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'd like to begin by offering a quick follow-up to Mr. Harmon's remarks about credibility, and in particular Mr. Harmon dealt with the categorisation of witnesses by the Defence while asserting in their brief that their witnesses came to "tell it like it is." I think it became apparent during the course of testimony that numbers of Defences witnesses came with their own issues, sometimes nationalism, sometimes over-identification with the accused. The point is not to reject them as a category, but to do what Mr. Harmon suggested the jurisprudence calls for; to examine them in light of all the evidence and all the factors. I'll mention a few examples quickly and then I'll move on. Witnesses such as Mr. Bjelica who admitted that he had previously stated: We wanted to have a complete break from the Muslims. We did not want to live with them, and we don't want to be buried near them. Witnesses like Mr. Milancic, who was confronted with his call at the 24th Assembly to take internationals as hostages, and then told the Court: Well, it seemed like a good idea at the time, basically. Witnesses like Mr. Milancic who also tried to persuade the Court that the Srbac had taken vigorous action to prosecute Serbs who committed crimes against Muslims, pointing to a particular example of a killing of a prominent Muslim. As it turned out, Your Honours will recall, that Serb was released after killing the prominent Muslim, went on to shoot four additional Muslims, four of whom -- two of whom were killed, and was not imprisoned until an incident in which he lightly wounded a Serb child. Or witnesses like Mr. Micic, who testified he'd never heard of the strategic objectives before coming to The Hague but was confronted with his presence at Assembly sessions when the strategic objectives were extensively discussed by Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, and in addition by a video which showed him discussing the strategic objectives with Mr. Maksimovic, indeed a video where the question was posed whether there was any other way to implement the strategic objectives other than war. On the other hand, there are witnesses like Mr. Kasagic, who talked about the need to reduce the Muslim population to 5 per cent, or Mr. Micic, who talked about his brother who was on the Bijeljina Crisis Staff, working together on that Crisis Staff with Mauzer. Or Mr. Vasic, who testified that the second strategic goal was a military goal. He said: "It was a military objective and in that sense a strategic objective of the Bosnian Serb forces to establish contiguous territory and prevent any border from separating the Serbian people." All of this, Your Honour, again, is not to suggest that Defence witnesses should be rejected as a category, but it just underscores what Mr. Harmon was saying, the need for the Court - and I'm sure the Court will do so - to evaluate their testimony in light of all the factors including all the evidence and accept or reject any parts of their testimony the Court considers credible. Your Honour, I'd like to turn next to the issue of genocide. In this case, as the Court is well aware, we consider a systematic campaign of chilling proportions and consequences that was bent on achieving the goal of Serb territory by the removal of Muslims and Croats at all costs. This campaign sought the acquisition of territories that were populated by those considered dangerous and undesirable and was fueled by the memory of historic tragedies and a sense of victimisation. The Court knows what happened, how Muslims and Croats were moved from the protections of law, subjected to forces determined to secure their disappearance, and the fate of many, many of whom were killed and many subjected to conditions likely to cause death. The Court must now answer the question whether these circumstances fall within the scope of genocide. The Defence notes in its brief that genocide has been called the crime of crimes, and therefore it urges it has a stigmatising effect and should not be diluted. It must be emphasised, however, that for that very reason the Court must not unduly restrict the application of genocide and therefore refrain from stigmatising conduct that properly falls within the Statute and has no place in a civilised world to which we must strive -- to which an increasingly armed planet must strive. Genocide, of course, Your Honour is a legal conclusion that rests on a combination of a prohibited act and intent; therefore, a vast killing campaign resulting in untold deaths may not constitute genocide, and on the other hand a far smaller number of deaths may do so. Fundamental inquiry is often intent. That inquiry, however, must not be confused with motive. While there may be a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- as was the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry. There may be, of course, a convergence of intent in motive, as was the case in the genocide of World War II; however, any number of motives may prompt an accused to engage in a prohibited act that falls within the Statute with an intent to destroy a protected group. It's no defence to say that genocidal intent is lacking because the accused's motive in destroying the group was, for example, acquisitory. Now, in this case, Your Honour, territory was to be acquired to the establishment of a criminal enterprise intended to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims and Croats by whatever means possible. In a moment I'll direct the Court to assertions that were made that if Bosnia declared independence it would lead to the annihilation of Bosnian Muslims and Croats. But let me first say this: It is evident that prohibited acts under Article 4(2) in this case were committed. So the issue is whether Mr. Krajisnik and, in this case, others had the intent to destroy a protected group. The determination of that intent may rest upon the circumstances surrounding the relevant acts, may also be gleaned from more direct evidence. Genocidal intent may be inferred from, among other things, the discriminatory intent of the accused, acts or utterances of the accused or his associates, and so on. Indeed, inference of genocidal intent may be drawn even where the individuals to whom the intent is attributable are not precisely identified, as in the Krstic case. But the most direct insight into intent may be provided by what perpetrators or those closest to them say, and I turn now to some of that evidence. You'll recall, of course, Dr. Karadzic's speech at the October 14th or October 15th session of the Assembly, when he referred to the possible extinction of the Muslims. Now, that has been interpreted by some in this case as referring to political rather than biological extinction, but a closer review of the evidence available to us makes clear that Dr. Karadzic referred to an intended physical destruction, and we cite the Court quickly to a number of intercepts with which I believe the Court is familiar. First, the intercept with Mr. Djogo two days before the speech, and I just direct the Court's attention to a few of the salient comments in that intercept. Djogo: "What's he thinking, to start a war in Sarajevo? Is he crazy?" He says again. Dr. Karadzic says: "They should be thrashed if they start a war. They'll disappear." Djogo: "There will be rivers of blood." Karadzic: "They will disappear, that people will disappear from the face of the earth if they start now." Karadzic continued in that conversation with remarks such as the fact that 300.000 Muslims in Sarajevo would die and the Muslims in Bosnia would disappear at the hands of the Serb forces. He said that Muslims would be up to their necks in blood and the Muslim people would disappear, the poor Muslims would disappear. And he also said, "Europe will be told to go fuck itself, not to come back until the job is finished." Now, the next day Dr. Karadzic reiterated the view that Muslims would be annihilated in a conversation with Mandic. In just a couple of days, he said, Sarajevo will be gone and there will be 500.000 dead. In one month Muslims will be annihilated in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He spoke to his brother the day after the Assembly session of the 14th and 15th, and he said: There will be war until their obliteration. None of their leaders would stay alive. Now, Your Honours, these remarks cannot be minimised as public rhetoric for political purposes because they were made outside of the public context. And indeed, Mr. Krajisnik had advised Dr. Karadzic in a conversation of September 4th, in which they agreed that Muslims would disappear and be annihilated, to simply say publicly that both Serbs and Muslims would suffer that fate. But the intercepts to which I just referred the Court are stunningly clear and unguarded expressions by Karadzic of the nature of the campaign that would be launched if Muslims pursued their intentions for independence. And indeed that's precisely how Dr. Karadzic's words were understood by other Bosnian Serbs in leadership positions. At the 4th Assembly Session regional leader Vukic said, to applause: "The EC recognition of Bosnia as an independent state would result in 'another Serbian uprising and there will be massive bloodshed in which some nations that have been subsequently created -'" and that means the Muslims, as we heard in this court -- "'will disappear altogether.'" And indeed, once the campaign began, these expressions continued. At the 17th Assembly in July, 1992, Dr. Karadzic said: "This conflict was roused in order to eliminate the Muslims. They think they are being nationally established, but in fact they are vanishing." Similarly, Dr. Kalinic, at the 16th Session, said, "Knowing who our enemies are, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily destroyed and crushed, which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people." Now, Your Honours, evidence of intent is found not only in the direct statements of elimination but other expressions of intent to eliminate a protected group may also provide such evidence. In that connection the Court can look to many comments with which the Court has been previously made aware, such as Dr. Karadzic's remarks that Muslims cannot live with others. We must be clear on that. Or: They'll overwhelm you with their birth-rate and their tricks. Or Mr. Krajisnik's call for pure territories, or Kupresanin explaining at the 24th Assembly that the war had been necessary because now Bosnia would be a predominantly Serb republic, and noting that Serbia should do the same to prevent Albanians and Muslims from taking over in Serbia. As the Appeals Chamber recognised in Krstic, there are a number of means apart from killing to secure the disappearance of a group. In certain circumstances, forcible transfer, if committed with the specific intent, can be one of the means to secure the physical disappearance of a protected group. And as mentioned, Your Honour, evidence must be considered in context. And I ask the Court to keep one additional aspect of context in mind. A recurring theme among the Bosnian Serbs was the very theme of genocide: The assertion that Muslims and Croats were threatening them with the same genocide they had suffered in World War II. And for those living in the past and captive to this mind-set, the destruction of the Muslims represented an anticipatory quid pro quo. As Ambassador Okun warned Karadzic: If you keep talking about genocide, you will commit a pre-emptive genocide. Your Honour, the genocidal intent of the Bosnian Serb leadership can be inferred from other aspects of evidence as well: Scale and pattern of the attacks, their intensity, the substantial number of Muslims killed, the detention of Muslims and Croats, their brutal treatment in those facilities and elsewhere, and the targeting of persons essential to the survival of the Muslims and Croats as a group are all factors that must be considered by the Court. The Court has received a great deal of evidence of killings of Muslims and Croat civilians and infliction of bodily harm in 1992 on a massive scale and also received considerable evidence on atrocious conditions in detention facilities. In addition, I ask the Court to keep in mind the considerable evidence about the forcible displacement and systematic transfer off the territory claimed by the Serbs, and the Court must assess this evidence in conjunction with the statements of the Bosnian Serb leadership anticipating the disappearance of the Muslims. With all those factors in mind, Your Honour, the Prosecution submits that the Court's conclusion must be that the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik, intended that the Muslims and Croats should physically disappear from the targeted territory and intended that the campaign which they led include a massive campaign of killings, bodily and mental harm, and detention in life-threatening conditions with the intention of securing the physical disappearance of Muslims and Croats. And the charge of genocide against Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour, has therefore been established. Your Honour, in my remaining time I'd like to address two issues, and that is the issue of sentencing and the issue of victim impact. I'll need only a very few words about victim impact. No one should attempt to capture the tragedy of the hundreds of thousands of victims in this case. Indeed, the scale of the impact of the victims in this case is most accurately reflected by the impossibility of attempting to fully assess it. We ask the Court not to think of a hundred victims or a thousand victims or hundreds of thousands of victims, for there was really one victim at a time over and over and over, each with his or her own tragedy and his or her own pain. Therefore, in assessing the impact in this case, Your Honours, each victim must be considered. Finally, Your Honour, I turn to the issue of sentencing, and what in the Prosecution's view and submission is appropriate for the crimes committed by Mr. Krajisnik. In making our determination on the appropriate sentence, we have considered various factors in aggravation and mitigation. I'd like to comment on those quickly. In respect of aggravating factors, it is our submission that there are three factors that aggravate the sentence. The first is abuse of authority. Mr. Krajisnik was an intelligent man, an educated man, a man who professed in this court to have the trust of Serbs and non-Serbs alike before the war. Yet, he used his positions of power not to protect Muslims and Croats from the harms that befell them, but instead to implement the campaign of -- massive campaign of persecution and destruction against the populations. It is our submission, therefore, that Mr. Krajisnik abused his position of authority and the trust of the civilian population and his sentence should be aggravated as a result. The second factor, Your Honour, is that Mr. Krajisnik's victims were vulnerable.
