The vast majority of those victims, of course, were non-Serb civilians, young and old alike, violently uprooted from their homes and settlements, abused, put into camps or cast out into the unknown with little or no means of survival at their disposal at that time. Bosnia was impoverished, the lives of its people were impoverished then and now. Mr. Krajisnik's sentence, we submit, should be aggravated because of the vulnerability of those victims. And I'd like to turn quickly to the third aggravating factor, the types of conduct for which Mr. Krajisnik is responsible: Killings, forcible expulsions, deportations, unlawful detentions, destruction of non-Serb homes, wholesale and systematic destruction of sacred sites, genocide, and the fact that the commission of these crimes was protracted. From the end of March 1992 until December 1992, the scale, Your Honour, and scope of those crimes and the length of time over which they were committed warrants an aggravating factor in sentencing. The Prosecution has also identified two factors in mitigation. The first factor recognised by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is that an accused with no prior convictions carries a factor that may be considered by the Court. Our position is that the weight of this factor, in light of the magnitude of the crimes committed, should be very little in this case in assessing an appropriate sentence for the conduct. The second factor is comportment in detention; another factor that the Prosecution submits is a technical basis for mitigation but has little relevance in light of the scale of crimes in this case. We accept that Mr. Krajisnik has conducted himself properly in detention, but again, in light of the massive nature of the crimes committed by the accused, it is our submission that this sentence should have little weight in mitigating the sentence. Accordingly, Your Honour, it's our submission as follows: Each count of the indictment individually, if found to be true, merits the highest possible sentence, regardless of the mode of liability. Therefore, based on the crimes committed by Mr. Krajisnik, the aggravated factors associated with them, the absence of substantial mitigating factors, it is our submission that Mr. Krajisnik should be sentenced to prison for life. That concludes my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I take it that it concludes the submissions of the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, you have informed the Chamber about what you'd wish the Chamber to have available tomorrow in order to be better able to follow. Hanson report. Just the report, or annexes to it as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't going to ask Your Honours to have everything that goes with the Hanson report. That would rather be a tall order. Your Honour, may I make it clear that the particular items which I've asked the Court to bring were -- because they are large items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If I referred to reports, I do only mean the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, they won't be the only items I refer to, but the other ones will be small items and I will take care of that and ensure they are put before the Court in a convenient way, but they are physically large items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Treanor report and also the report only, as far as --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you referred to the army report as we find it in the glossary in the OTP. For the army report, I find two sources, the first one being Exhibit P64A, tab 6, which, at least what I've got under 64A.6 is as a matter of fact not a report on the army, but it is P529 tab 255 seems to be an analysis --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but there are two sources, one rather misleading, it seems, in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, to be frank, Your Honour, I thought the Trial Chamber would take its pick of the one that produced the documents, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- it seems it has done just that, yes, but that's the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the reference -- I've got a copy of it on which it says at the front P64A, binder 26, tab 779. If that offers anybody an alternative source, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it that P529, tab 25 -- that is only one document and that is what you call the -- and what the Prosecution calls the army report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then for further exhibits you would like to refer to, I have to make a confession, not on all computers in this court-room easily accessible for everyone are all the exhibits. Although I would have 99 per cent, for example, one of the things that would not be in my computer is, surprisingly, the Treanor report itself, but I will get that. But at least on one of the computers here it would be easy to produce most of the evidence, so there's no need to have it copied again. If you would not be surprised if the other Judges would look from the left and to the right on my screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, after two and a half years, no, I wouldn't be surprised. No, Your Honour is correct. But, Your Honour, I will take care of the logistics of what probably will only be two- or three-page exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the Chamber is also a bit concerned about the quantity of paper that's used in this courtroom. If you can do without, that would be -- if we have it on our screen, then it certainly is worth trying. Then if there's nothing else for tomorrow --
